name: Venus Flytrap
range: Coastal bogs of North & South Carolina
entry: Its hinged leaves snap shut in about a tenth of a second, but only when two trigger hairs are touched within about 20 seconds. This double check keeps it from wasting energy on falling raindrops.

name: California Pitcher Plant
range: Mountain seeps of N. California & S. Oregon
entry: Light shines through pale windows in its hood. Trapped insects fly at these false exits again and again until they tire and tumble into the fluid below. It keeps its roots in cold, flowing spring water.

name: Common Milkweed
entry: Its milky sap is loaded with heart-stopping toxins. In autumn each seed pod splits open and releases hundreds of seeds that ride the wind on tufts of white silk.

name: Monarch Butterfly
range: All of N. America; winters in Michoacán, Mexico
entry: Toxins it ate from milkweed as a caterpillar keep it bitter to birds for life. The autumn generation flies up to 3,000 miles to fir forests in central Mexico, a place none of them has ever seen.

name: Tiger Swallowtail Caterpillar
entry: The big false eyes on its swollen front end make it look like a small green snake. When bothered, it pops out a forked orange organ that gives off a foul smell.

name: Western Tiger Swallowtail
entry: Groups of males gather on damp mud to sip salts and minerals. The long tails on its hindwings draw a bird's beak away from its body.

name: White-lined Sphinx Caterpillar
entry: It has a harmless horn at the end of its body. After wet desert springs, millions can hatch at once and march across roads looking for more plants to eat.

name: White-lined Sphinx
entry: It hovers in front of flowers and beats its wings so fast that people often mistake it for a hummingbird. At dusk it unrolls a long tongue to sip nectar from deep flowers.

name: Malachite Caterpillar
range: S. Florida & Texas to Central America
entry: Its black body bristles with red-based spines, and two long horns sprout from its head. It feeds on the leaves of plants in the acanthus family.

name: Malachite
range: S. Florida & Texas to Central America
entry: Its wings carry bright green panels that shine like the mineral it is named after. It sips from rotting fruit, bat droppings and dead animals on the forest floor.

name: Common Sunflower
entry: Young flower heads follow the sun from east to west and swing back overnight. Once grown, they settle facing east, which warms them in the morning and brings in more bees.

name: Chili Pepper
range: Native to Mexico; now grown worldwide
entry: The capsaicin in its fruit burns the mouths of mammals, but birds cannot feel it at all. Birds swallow the seeds whole and spread them far away. People in Mexico began growing it more than 6,000 years ago.

name: Giant Sequoia
range: Western slope of the Sierra Nevada, California
entry: It is the largest single tree on Earth by volume. Its bark can be two feet thick and shrugs off fire, and the heat of a wildfire helps its cones open and drop their seeds.

name: Coast Redwood
entry: It is the tallest living thing on Earth. One tree, named Hyperion, stands about 380 feet high. In the dry summer its needles comb fog from the sea air, and the water drips down to its roots.

name: Western Joshua Tree
entry: Only yucca moths can pollinate it. The moth packs its pollen into a ball and lays eggs in the flower, and its caterpillars eat some of the seeds. Neither the tree nor the moth can reproduce without the other.

name: Saguaro
entry: It may be 50 to 100 years old before it grows its first arm. After a heavy rain its pleated trunk swells like an accordion to store hundreds of gallons of water.

name: Bunny Ears Cactus
entry: It has no long spines. Instead it is covered in soft-looking dots of tiny barbed bristles that come loose at a touch and are very hard to pull out of skin.

name: Resurrection Plant
entry: In a drought it curls into a brown, dead-looking ball and can lose nearly all of its water. When rain returns it unrolls and turns green again within hours.

name: Ghost Pipe
entry: It has no chlorophyll and cannot make its own food. It steals sugar from underground fungi, which get it from tree roots. It turns black soon after it is picked.

name: Avocado
range: Native to S. Mexico & Central America
entry: Its huge seed may once have been spread by giant ground sloths and other megafauna that swallowed the fruit whole. Those animals died out long ago, but the tree still makes fruit sized for them.

name: Cacao Tree
entry: Its flowers and pods grow straight out of its trunk, and tiny midges pollinate the flowers. The Maya and Aztecs used its beans as money and made them into a bitter drink. Its name means "food of the gods."

name: Pink Lady's Slipper
range: Forests of E. Canada & the E. United States
entry: Bees push into its pink pouch looking for nectar, but there is none. The only way out is a narrow exit that brushes pollen onto their backs. Its dust-like seeds need a fungus to sprout.

name: American Lotus
entry: Water beads up and rolls off its leaves, carrying dirt away with it. Its hard seeds can lie buried in mud for decades before they sprout. The dried seed head looks like a showerhead.

name: Red Mangrove
range: Florida, the Gulf Coast & the Caribbean
entry: Arching prop roots hold it up in salt water and filter out most of the salt. Its seeds sprout while still on the tree, then drop as long, pencil-shaped seedlings that can float for months.

name: Water Horsetail
entry: Its hollow, jointed stems are stiffened with silica, and horsetails were once used to scrub pots. Its relatives grew as tall as trees over 300 million years ago, and their remains became much of today's coal.

name: American Fly Agaric
entry: This western form of the classic toadstool has a red cap dotted with yellowish warts. It is poisonous. Underground it wraps around the roots of pines and birches, trading minerals for sugar.

name: Chicken of the Woods
range: Hardwood forests of eastern North America
entry: It grows as bright orange and yellow shelves on oak trees and rots the wood from within. When cooked, its texture is said to be a lot like chicken.

name: Common Bird's Nest Fungus
entry: Its tiny cups hold egg-like packets of spores. When a raindrop lands in the cup, the packets are flung several feet, trailing a sticky cord that snags on nearby plants.

name: Cedar-apple Rust
entry: It needs two different hosts to finish its life cycle. On juniper trees it forms brown galls that sprout orange, jelly-like horns after spring rain. These release spores that infect apple trees.

name: Blushing Rock Tripe
entry: It is a lichen: a fungus and an alga living as one. It clings to bare rock by a single central stalk. Starving Arctic explorers, including John Franklin's party in 1821, survived by eating rock tripe.

name: White Carnival Candy Slime Mold
entry: It is not a plant, an animal or a fungus. It spends most of its life as creeping cells that eat bacteria, then rises into tiny stalks of gray spore fluff. Some slime molds can find the shortest path through a maze.

name: Watermelon Snow
entry: This single-celled green alga shields itself from sunlight with red pigment, tinting summer snow pink. The darker snow soaks up more heat, so it speeds up melting. Some say it smells faintly of watermelon.

name: Giant Kelp
range: Pacific coast, Alaska to Baja California
entry: It can grow up to two feet in a single day. Gas-filled floats lift its blades toward the sunlight, forming underwater forests that shelter hundreds of kinds of animals.

name: Bullet Ant
entry: Its sting ranks among the most painful of any insect. Victims describe waves of burning pain that can last a full day, as if they had been shot.

name: Mexican Honeypot Ant
range: Deserts of the SW US & N. Mexico
entry: Some workers, called repletes, are fed nectar until their abdomens swell to the size of a pea. They hang from the nest ceiling as living food jars that feed the colony during drought.

name: Thistledown Velvet Ant
range: Deserts of the SW US & N. Mexico
entry: It is not an ant but a wingless female wasp. Its long white hair makes it look like a fluffy creosote bush seed. It has a very painful sting and a tough, hard body.

name: American Bumble Bee
entry: Tiny hairs on its body can sense the weak electric fields around flowers, which may help it tell which ones were just visited. On cold mornings it warms up by shivering its flight muscles.

name: Bald-faced Hornet
entry: It is actually a kind of yellowjacket. The colony builds a paper nest as big as a basketball from chewed wood. When defending it, a worker can squirt venom at an attacker's eyes.

name: Giant Stag Beetle
entry: Males use their huge, antler-like jaws to wrestle rivals. Its larvae spend years chewing through rotting logs before they become adults.

name: Desert Ironclad Beetle
range: Deserts of the SW US & NW Mexico
entry: Its wing covers are fused into a tough shell, so it cannot fly. A powdery blue wax on its back helps it hold in water. When touched, it drops and plays dead.

name: American Burying Beetle
range: Scattered sites in the central & eastern US
entry: A pair buries the body of a small dead animal, strips off the fur and coats it to slow rotting. Both parents stay to feed their larvae, which is rare among beetles.

name: Convergent Lady Beetle
entry: It can eat around 50 aphids a day. In winter, millions pile together on mountain slopes. If grabbed, it oozes bitter yellow blood from its leg joints.

name: Glassy-winged Sharpshooter
entry: It drinks huge amounts of watery plant sap and can excrete up to 300 times its body weight in a day. It flicks each droplet away with a tiny catapult on its tail end.

name: Point Conception Jerusalem Cricket
entry: It is neither a cricket nor from Jerusalem. It spends most of its life underground and finds a mate by drumming its abdomen on the soil. Scientists only named this species recently.

name: Grizzled Mantis
entry: Its mottled gray body blends almost perfectly with lichen-covered bark. It presses flat and stays still until prey wanders close, then strikes with its spiked front legs.

name: American Giant Water Bug
entry: Its nickname is the toe-biter. It injects saliva that turns the insides of fish and frogs to liquid, then drinks them. It breathes through a snorkel-like tube at its rear.

name: Giant Mayfly
entry: It spends up to two years underwater as a nymph, but lives only a day or two as a winged adult with no working mouth. Its swarms can be big enough to show up on weather radar.

name: Widow Skimmer
range: Most of the US & southern Canada
entry: It snatches flying insects out of the air with its legs. Dragonflies like it catch prey on most of their hunting attempts, which makes them some of the most successful predators on Earth.

name: Urania Swallowtail Moth
entry: Unlike most moths, it flies by day. Its green and black wings shimmer because their scales bend light rather than hold pigment. Huge numbers migrate across Central America when their food plants turn toxic.

name: Lone Star Tick
entry: The female has a single white spot on her back. Its bite can make some people allergic to red meat, a condition called alpha-gal syndrome.

name: Brown Recluse
entry: It has a dark violin shape on its back and only six eyes, set in three pairs. It is shy and hides in dry, undisturbed corners. Bites are rare, but they can damage skin.

name: Western Black Widow
entry: The female is glossy black with a red hourglass under her belly. Drop for drop, her venom is more potent than a rattlesnake's, but she injects only a tiny amount.

name: Bold Jumping Spider
entry: Its big front eyes give it some of the sharpest vision of any spider. It can study its prey, plan a roundabout route, and leap many times its body length while trailing a silk safety line.

name: Mexican Redknee Tarantula
entry: Females can live 25 to 30 years. When threatened, it kicks a cloud of barbed hairs off its abdomen that irritate a predator's eyes and skin.

name: Western Forest Scorpion
entry: Like all scorpions, it glows blue-green under ultraviolet light. A mother carries her newborn young on her back until they molt for the first time.

name: Black-and-gold Flat Millipede
entry: When disturbed, it oozes a fluid that releases hydrogen cyanide and smells like almonds. Its bold colors warn predators that it is not worth eating.

name: Common Desert Centipede
entry: Its venomous fangs are really its first pair of legs, reshaped over time into claws. It hunts at night and eats insects, spiders and even small lizards.

name: Jamaican Velvet Worm
entry: It shoots two jets of sticky slime from its head to trap insects, then bites and eats them. Velvet worms have kept much the same body plan for hundreds of millions of years.

name: American Lobster
range: Atlantic coast, Labrador to North Carolina
entry: It has two different claws: a heavy crusher and a sharp pincer. Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper. The largest one on record weighed over 44 pounds.

name: Atlantic Horseshoe Crab
range: Atlantic & Gulf coasts, Maine to the Yucatán
entry: It is more closely related to spiders than to crabs. Its blue blood is used to test medicines and vaccines for harmful bacteria. Its body plan has barely changed in about 450 million years.

name: Pacific Acorn Barnacle
range: Pacific coast, Alaska to Baja California
entry: It glues its head to a rock and spends its life kicking food into its mouth with feathery legs. Because it can never move, it has the longest reproductive organ for its size of any animal.

name: Giant Pacific Octopus
range: North Pacific coast, Alaska to California
entry: It is the largest octopus in the world. It can change its color and skin texture in an instant, solve puzzles and open jars. Each of its arms has about 280 suckers that can taste what they touch.

name: Pacific Banana Slug
entry: It is one of the largest land slugs in the world. Its slime can numb the tongue of any animal that tries to eat it. It recycles the forest floor by eating dead leaves, mushrooms and droppings.

name: Hind's Chiton
range: Pacific coast, Alaska to Baja California
entry: Its tongue is lined with teeth capped in magnetite, an iron mineral, making them some of the hardest teeth of any animal. It uses them to scrape algae off rocks.

name: Eastern Oyster
entry: A single oyster can filter up to 50 gallons of water a day. Young oysters settle on older shells, building reefs over time. Many start life as males and later become females.

name: Lion's Mane Jelly
entry: It is one of the largest jellies in the world. One found in 1870 had a bell over seven feet wide and tentacles about 120 feet long, longer than a blue whale.

name: Christmas Tree Worm
entry: It uses its two colorful spiral crowns to breathe and catch food. At the first sign of danger it pulls them into its tube in a flash. It can live in the same coral head for decades.

name: Whale Shark
range: Warm oceans, incl. the Gulf of California & Gulf of Mexico
entry: It is the largest fish in the world, yet it eats tiny plankton and fish eggs. The pattern of spots on each shark is unique, like a fingerprint.

name: Scalloped Hammerhead
range: Warm coastal waters of both coasts
entry: Its wide head spreads out its electric-sensing pores, helping it find stingrays buried in sand. By day, hundreds gather in schools around underwater mountains.

name: Greenland Shark
entry: It may live more than 270 years, longer than any other known vertebrate. It cruises at about a mile per hour and may not mature until it is around 150 years old.

name: Pacific Hagfish
range: Pacific coast, Alaska to Baja California
entry: It has a skull but no jaws and no true backbone. When grabbed, it releases slime that swells into buckets of goo, then ties itself in a knot to scrape itself clean.

name: Atlantic Bluefin Tuna
range: Atlantic, Canada to the Gulf of Mexico
entry: Unlike most fish, it keeps its body warmer than the water around it. This lets it hunt in cold northern seas and swim across the entire Atlantic Ocean.

name: Common Mola
range: Temperate & tropical oceans off both coasts
entry: It is one of the heaviest bony fish in the world. After deep dives it floats on its side at the surface to warm up. A female can carry around 300 million eggs.

name: Longsnout Seahorse
entry: The male carries the eggs in a pouch until they hatch. It holds on to sea grass with its tail and sucks up tiny shrimp through its tube-shaped snout.

name: Devils Hole Pupfish
range: One cave pool: Devils Hole, Nevada
entry: The whole species lives in a single water-filled cave pool in the Nevada desert. It survives in water around 93°F that holds little oxygen. In 2013, only 35 were counted.

name: Red-eyed Tree Frog
entry: It sleeps by day with its bright colors tucked away. When disturbed, it suddenly flashes red eyes, blue sides and orange feet, which startles a predator long enough for it to escape.

name: Gliding Leaf Frog
entry: Its large webbed hands and feet act as parachutes, so it can glide from tree to tree. It lays eggs on leaves above ponds, and the tadpoles drop into the water when they hatch.

name: Emerald Glass Frog
entry: Its belly is see-through, so its heart and organs are visible from below. Males guard eggs laid on leaves over streams and wrestle rivals while hanging upside down.

name: Strawberry Poison Dart Frog
entry: Its poison comes from the ants and mites it eats. The mother carries each tadpole to a tiny pool inside a plant, then returns to feed it her own unfertilized eggs.

name: Variable Harlequin Frog
entry: A deadly skin fungus wiped it out across most of its range in the 1980s and 1990s, and it was feared extinct. Small groups were later rediscovered, and it now survives in only a few places.

name: Red-spotted Newt
entry: It lives in three stages: a larva in the water, a bright orange land form called a red eft, and a green adult back in the water. Its skin carries a toxin that makes it dangerous to eat.

name: Mexican Burrowing Toad
entry: It spends most of its life underground and comes up only after heavy rain. Unlike other frogs, its tongue shoots straight out of its mouth to lap up ants and termites. When calling, it puffs up like a balloon.

name: American Alligator
entry: It builds a mound nest of rotting plants, and the warmth of the nest decides whether the babies hatch male or female. Once hunted to near extinction, it recovered and left the endangered list in 1987.

name: Common Basilisk
entry: Nicknamed the Jesus Christ lizard, it sprints across water on its hind legs by slapping the surface with its broad toes. Young ones can run farther on water than adults.

name: Green Iguana
range: Mexico to South America; introduced in Florida
entry: A pale scale on top of its head, called a third eye, senses light and shadow from above and warns it of hawks. It eats mostly leaves and can fall from high branches without getting hurt.

name: Texas Horned Lizard
entry: When a coyote or dog attacks, it can squirt blood from its eyes up to five feet. The blood tastes foul to canines. It feeds mainly on harvester ants.

name: Gila Monster
entry: It chews venom into its prey instead of injecting it. A compound in its saliva led to a diabetes medicine. It can eat a third of its body weight at once and may need only a few meals a year.

name: Western Diamond-backed Rattlesnake
entry: Pits between its eyes and nostrils sense heat, so it can strike warm-bodied prey in total darkness. It adds a new segment to its rattle each time it sheds its skin.

name: Sidewinder
entry: It moves sideways in looping curves that keep only two small parts of its body touching the hot sand. The horn-like scales over its eyes may help shade them from the sun.

name: Texas Coralsnake
entry: Its red and yellow bands touch, a warning of its powerful venom. It hunts other snakes and spends much of its time hidden under leaf litter.

name: California Kingsnake
entry: It resists rattlesnake venom and often hunts rattlesnakes, squeezing them until they stop breathing. Its bands can be black and white, brown and cream, or run lengthwise as stripes.

name: Common Snapping Turtle
entry: Its shell is too small to hide in, so it defends itself with a powerful beak and a long, fast neck. It can spend the whole winter under the ice, taking in oxygen through its skin.

name: Leatherback Sea Turtle
range: All oceans; nests in Florida & the Caribbean
entry: It is the largest turtle alive, with a soft, leathery shell. Its huge body holds in heat, so it can swim into cold water off Canada to feed on jellyfish. It can dive deeper than 3,000 feet.

name: Bald Eagle
entry: It builds the largest nests of any North American bird and adds to them year after year. One nest in Florida weighed over two tons. It often steals fish from ospreys.

name: Peregrine Falcon
entry: When it dives from high in the sky it can top 200 miles per hour, making it the fastest animal on Earth. The pesticide DDT nearly wiped it out in North America, but it has since come back.

name: Great Horned Owl
entry: Soft, fringed feathers let it fly almost silently. It is one of the few animals that often hunts skunks, since it has a poor sense of smell.

name: Snowy Owl
range: Arctic tundra; winters south into the US
entry: It hunts in the round-the-clock daylight of the Arctic summer. In years when lemmings are plentiful, a pair may raise a dozen chicks. It can hear prey moving under the snow.

name: Burrowing Owl
range: Western N. America, Florida & Mexico southward
entry: It nests underground, often in old prairie dog burrows. When cornered, its chicks hiss like a rattlesnake. It spreads animal dung around its burrow to lure in dung beetles to eat.

name: Common Raven
entry: It is one of the smartest birds. It can solve puzzles, plan ahead and remember people who treated it badly. It can mimic other birds, car engines and even human speech.

name: Greater Roadrunner
entry: It can run about 20 miles per hour. It kills rattlesnakes and lizards by grabbing them and slamming them against the ground. On cold mornings it warms up by sunning a patch of dark skin on its back.

name: Purple-throated Mountain-gem
range: Mountains of Nicaragua, Costa Rica & Panama
entry: This tiny hummingbird lives in cloud forests. Its heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute in flight. The male flashes a purple throat and a blue crown.

name: Roseate Spoonbill
range: Florida, the Gulf Coast & Latin America
entry: It sweeps its spoon-shaped bill side to side through shallow water and snaps it shut on anything it touches. Its pink color comes from pigments in the shrimp and crabs it eats.

name: Keel-billed Toucan
entry: Its huge rainbow bill is light because it is mostly hollow. Sending blood to the bill helps it shed body heat, like a radiator. It is the national bird of Belize.

name: Common Potoo
entry: By day it perches upright on a broken branch and looks just like part of the tree. Even with its eyes shut, it can watch through small notches in its eyelids. At night its mournful song rings through the forest.

name: Tufted Puffin
entry: In summer it grows golden plumes over its eyes and a bright orange bill. It uses its wings to fly underwater and can carry many small fish crosswise in its bill at once.

name: Greater Sage-Grouse
range: Sagebrush of the western US & SW Canada
entry: At dawn in spring, males gather at dancing grounds, puff out their white chests and pop two yellow air sacs. In winter it eats almost nothing but sagebrush leaves.

name: Turkey Vulture
entry: Unusually for a bird, it can smell a dead animal from more than a mile away. Its stomach acid is strong enough to destroy anthrax and other deadly germs in rotting meat.

name: Canada Goose
entry: Flocks fly in a V shape and take turns at the front to save energy. Pairs usually mate for life and fiercely defend their goslings.

name: Grizzly Bear
range: Alaska, W. Canada & the northern Rockies
entry: It can smell food from miles away and run up to 35 miles per hour. The hump on its shoulders is a mass of muscle that powers its long claws for digging up roots and ground squirrels.

name: Polar Bear
entry: Its fur is not white but clear and hollow, and the skin underneath is black. It spends most of its life on sea ice hunting seals and can swim for days without resting.

name: American Bison
entry: It is the heaviest land animal in North America. Tens of millions once roamed the plains, but by the late 1800s fewer than a thousand remained. In winter it swings its huge head to sweep snow off the grass.

name: Gray Wolf
entry: It lives in family packs led by a breeding pair. Wolves howl to gather the pack and warn rivals, and a howl can carry up to 10 miles over open ground.

name: Red Fox
entry: It can hear a mouse squeak from 100 feet away. Some researchers think it uses Earth's magnetic field to aim its pounces, since it hits its target most often when facing northeast.

name: Common Raccoon
entry: Its front paws have extremely sensitive fingertips, and wetting them may make them even more sensitive. It can pick locks, open latches and remember the solution to a puzzle for years.

name: Virginia Opossum
range: Eastern & central US, Mexico & the Pacific coast
entry: When badly frightened, it goes limp, drools and gives off a smell of death. It is North America's only marsupial, and it resists the venom of many snakes.

name: Striped Skunk
range: The US, southern Canada & northern Mexico
entry: It can spray a sulfur-scented oil up to 10 feet with good aim. Before spraying, it stamps its feet and raises its tail as a warning. The smell can carry more than a mile.

name: American Beaver
entry: It builds dams that turn streams into ponds, creating wetlands for many other animals. Its front teeth are orange because they are hardened with iron, and they never stop growing.

name: Nine-banded Armadillo
entry: A mother almost always gives birth to four identical young, all from a single egg. It can hold its breath for six minutes and walk across the bottom of a stream.

name: Wolverine
range: Northern Canada, Alaska & the high Rockies
entry: Though only the size of a medium dog, it can chase bears and wolves away from a kill. Its huge, snowshoe-like paws let it travel dozens of miles a day through deep snow.

name: Jaguar
range: Mexico to Argentina; rare visitor to Arizona
entry: It has the strongest bite for its size of any big cat. Instead of going for the throat, it often bites straight through its prey's skull, and it can crack turtle shells. It is a strong, eager swimmer.

name: Mountain Goat
entry: Its hooves have hard edges and soft, grippy pads that cling to steep, icy cliffs. Despite its name, it is not a true goat.

name: Bighorn Sheep
entry: Rams charge each other at up to 20 miles per hour and clash horns with a crack that echoes off the mountains. A ram's horns can weigh more than all the other bones in its body.

name: Groundhog
entry: It is a true hibernator. In winter its heart slows from about 80 beats a minute to just 5, and its body temperature drops to a few degrees above freezing.

name: Northern Collared Lemming
range: Arctic tundra of Canada, Alaska & Greenland
entry: It is the only rodent that turns white in winter. Each winter it also grows large, two-pointed claws on its front feet for digging through snow.

name: Common Vampire Bat
entry: Heat sensors on its nose find blood vessels close to the skin, and its saliva keeps blood from clotting. If a roostmate fails to feed, it will share a meal with it, and the favor is later returned.

name: Brown-throated Three-toed Sloth
entry: It moves so slowly that algae grows in its fur and tints it green for camouflage. It climbs down from its tree only about once a week to go to the bathroom.

name: Mantled Howler Monkey
entry: Its howls are among the loudest calls of any land animal and can carry for miles through the forest. It eats mostly leaves and spends much of the day resting to digest them.

name: West Indian Manatee
range: Florida, the Gulf Coast & the Caribbean
entry: It spends up to eight hours a day grazing on sea grass. Its worn-down molars fall out at the front while new ones move forward to replace them, all its life.

name: Blue Whale
range: All oceans, including both North American coasts
entry: It is the largest animal known to have ever lived. Its heart is about the size of a golf cart, and its calls are among the loudest sounds made by any animal. It can eat 4 tons of krill a day.

name: Orca
range: All oceans, especially the Pacific Northwest
entry: It lives in close family pods, and each pod has its own set of calls, like a dialect. Different groups specialize in salmon, seals or even other whales, and they teach their hunting methods to their young.

name: Narwhal
entry: Its long spiral tusk is actually a tooth that grows out through its upper lip. The tusk has millions of nerve endings and may sense changes in the water. It can dive nearly a mile deep.

name: Atlantic Walrus
entry: It uses its long tusks to haul its huge body out of the water onto the ice. It finds clams on the dark sea floor with its sensitive whiskers, then sucks them out of their shells.

name: Queen of the Andes
entry: It grows as a spiky rosette for 80 years or more, then sends up a flower spike over 30 feet tall covered in thousands of blossoms. After this single bloom, the whole plant dies.

name: Giant Water Lily
entry: Its round leaves grow up to ten feet across and can hold the weight of a small child. Its flower opens white on the first night, traps beetles inside until morning, then reopens pink to release them covered in pollen.

name: Brazil Nut Tree
entry: Its seeds grow inside a pod as hard as a coconut that can weigh over four pounds and falls from 150 feet. Only agoutis can gnaw the pods open, and they bury seeds that grow into new trees. Its flowers are pollinated by large orchid bees.

name: Rubber Tree
entry: When its bark is cut, it bleeds a milky latex that becomes natural rubber. In the late 1800s, demand for tires and hoses set off the Amazon rubber boom. Most of the world's natural rubber still comes from this tree.

name: Cinchona
entry: Its bark contains quinine, the first effective medicine against malaria. Quinine also gives tonic water its bitter taste. The cinchona tree appears on the national coat of arms of Peru.

name: Ayahuasca Vine
entry: This woody vine climbs high into the rainforest canopy. Indigenous peoples of the Amazon brew it with other plants into a ceremonial drink used in healing and spiritual rituals.

name: Potato
range: Domesticated in the Andes of Peru & Bolivia
entry: People in the Andes began farming potatoes about 8,000 years ago and developed thousands of varieties. Its leaves and green skin are poisonous. It is now one of the most important food crops in the world.

name: Monkey Puzzle Tree
entry: Its branches are covered in sharp, overlapping leaves like a reptile's scales. Its family grew alongside the dinosaurs. It got its name when an English visitor joked that climbing it would puzzle a monkey.

name: Chilean Puya
entry: Its leaves are lined with hooked spines that snag birds and sheep that wander in. Some scientists think the animals that die there fertilize the plant, earning it the nickname sheep-eating plant.

name: Monkey Orchid
entry: Its flower looks remarkably like a monkey's face. The genus name Dracula means little dragon, for the flowers' long, fang-like tails. Despite its looks, it smells like ripe oranges.

name: Hot Lips
entry: Its bright red bracts look like a pair of puckered lips. They attract hummingbirds and butterflies before opening to reveal small white flowers inside.

name: Cannonball Tree
entry: Its round, woody fruits hang from its trunk like cannonballs and can weigh 20 pounds each. When they fall, they sometimes crack open with a bang and release a foul smell.

name: Copiapoa
entry: It lives in the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, where some spots go years without rain. It survives on moisture from coastal fog. Its chalky white skin reflects the harsh sun.

name: Llareta
range: High Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Chile & Argentina
entry: It grows as a dense green cushion so firm it looks like moss-covered rock. It grows only about half an inch a year, and some are thought to be thousands of years old.

name: Pineapple
entry: It is a bromeliad, and each fruit forms from over 100 flowers fused together. It contains bromelain, an enzyme that breaks down protein, which is why eating a lot of it can make your mouth sting.

name: Yerba Mate
entry: Its leaves are dried and steeped to make mate, a caffeine-rich drink shared from a gourd through a metal straw. It is the national drink of Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

name: Alerce
entry: One alerce in Chile was found to be over 3,600 years old, making it among the oldest trees on Earth. It can grow over 150 feet tall. Its rot-resistant wood was so valued that logging nearly wiped it out.

name: Lobster-claw Heliconia
entry: Its hanging red-and-yellow bracts look like a chain of lobster claws. Hummingbirds with curved bills sip nectar from its tube-shaped flowers. Small pools of water inside the bracts shelter tiny insects.

name: Sensitive Plant
entry: When touched, its leaves fold up within seconds and its stems droop. In one experiment, plants that were dropped over and over learned to stop folding and remembered it for weeks.

name: Darwin's Fungus
range: Southern beech forests of Chile & Argentina
entry: It grows on southern beech trees as bright orange balls covered in dimples like golf balls. Charles Darwin collected it in Tierra del Fuego and noted that local people ate it.

name: Zombie-ant Fungus
entry: It infects carpenter ants and takes control of their bodies. The ant climbs a plant, bites down on a leaf vein and dies there. A stalk then sprouts from its head and rains spores onto ants below.

name: Leafcutter Fungus
range: Leafcutter ant nests across tropical America
entry: This fungus lives only inside leafcutter ant nests. The ants feed it chewed leaves, and it grows swollen tips that the ants eat. The ants and the fungus have farmed together for millions of years.

name: Cinnabar Bracket
range: Dead wood across tropical South America
entry: This bright orange-red shelf fungus grows on fallen branches across the tropics. Its color comes from a pigment called cinnabarin. Scientists use its enzymes to break down pollutants such as textile dyes.

name: Blue Morpho Caterpillar
entry: It is red-brown with bright yellow-green patches and tufts of irritating hairs. When disturbed, it releases a smell like rancid butter to put off predators.

name: Blue Morpho
entry: Its wings shine a brilliant blue because tiny scales reflect light, not because of pigment. With its wings closed, it shows brown undersides with eyespots, so it seems to flash in and out of sight as it flies.

name: Hercules Beetle Larva
entry: The grub spends up to two years feeding in rotting logs and can weigh around four ounces, making it one of the heaviest insect larvae in the world.

name: Hercules Beetle
entry: It is one of the longest beetles in the world, and more than half of a male's length can be horn. Males use their pincer-like horns to lift rivals and throw them off branches.

name: Titan Beetle
entry: It is one of the largest beetles in the world, over six inches long. Its jaws are strong enough to snap a pencil. Its larvae have never been found, and scientists think they live deep inside rotting wood.

name: Leafcutter Ant
entry: Workers cut pieces of leaves and carry them home, but they do not eat them. They use them to grow a fungus garden, which feeds the colony. A single nest can hold millions of ants.

name: Army Ant
entry: A colony of up to a million ants swarms across the forest floor, eating every insect it catches. It has no permanent nest. Instead, workers link their bodies to build a living camp and bridges over gaps.

name: Glasswing Butterfly
range: Central America to northern South America
entry: Its wings are almost completely clear, like panes of glass, because tiny structures on their surface stop light from reflecting. This makes it very hard for birds to spot in flight.

name: Owl Butterfly
entry: Huge eyespots on the undersides of its wings look like an owl's eyes. It flies mostly at dusk and feeds on rotting fruit.

name: Brazilian Treehopper
entry: It wears a bizarre helmet with four hairy balls on stalks, like a tiny helicopter. Scientists still are not sure what it is for, though it may confuse predators or mimic a fungus that attacks insects.

name: Peanut-head Bug
entry: Its huge, hollow head looks like a tiny alligator's head, complete with fake teeth and eyes. When threatened, it flashes big eyespots on its hindwings and releases a skunky smell.

name: Kissing Bug
entry: It bites sleeping people near the lips and eyes at night. Its droppings can carry the parasite that causes Chagas disease, which can damage the heart years later.

name: Human Botfly
entry: It catches a mosquito and glues its eggs onto it. When the mosquito bites a mammal, the warmth makes the eggs hatch, and the larvae burrow into the skin to grow.

name: Orchid Bee
range: Tropical forests of Central & South America
entry: This shiny metallic bee comes in brilliant green, blue and gold. Males collect scents from orchids and store them in pouches on their legs to make their own perfume for attracting females.

name: Postman Butterfly
entry: Unlike most butterflies, it eats pollen as well as nectar, which helps it live for months. It is toxic to birds, and many unrelated butterflies copy its red and black pattern.

name: Headlight Beetle
entry: Two glowing green spots on its back look like headlights, and it shines bright enough to read by. It flips itself into the air with a loud click when placed on its back.

name: Railroad Worm
entry: This beetle larva glows red from its head and green from rows of lights along its sides, like a train at night. It is the only land creature known to make red light, which may let it see prey that cannot see red.

name: Peacock Katydid
entry: With wings folded, it looks exactly like a dead leaf. When disturbed, it throws open its wings to reveal a pair of huge eyespots, and it may rub its wings to make a hissing sound.

name: Snake-mimic Hawk Moth
entry: Its caterpillar is famous for puffing up the front of its body into the shape of a snake's head, complete with fake eyes, and even swaying and striking like a real snake. The adult is a fast, streamlined hawk moth that hovers at flowers.

name: Giant Patagonian Bumblebee
entry: It is the largest bumblebee in the world, covered in fluffy orange fur. It has been nicknamed the flying mouse. Its numbers have crashed since European bumblebees were brought to the region.

name: Harlequin Beetle
entry: Males have front legs longer than their whole bodies. Tiny pseudoscorpions ride under its wing covers to travel between trees, hopping off to hunt mites.

name: Goliath Birdeater
entry: It is the heaviest spider in the world, with legs spanning about a foot. Despite its name, it rarely eats birds, feeding mostly on worms, insects and frogs. It hisses by rubbing the bristles on its legs.

name: Brazilian Wandering Spider
entry: It does not build a web but wanders the forest floor at night hunting. It raises its front legs in a warning pose. Its venom is dangerous, but scientists are studying it to make new medicines.

name: Amazon Whip Spider
entry: It is neither a spider nor a scorpion. It feels its way through the dark with a pair of very long, thin front legs and can find its way home through the forest at night. It has no venom and no silk.

name: Brazilian Yellow Scorpion
entry: Females reproduce without males, making copies of themselves. This lets a single scorpion start a new colony, and it has spread into Brazilian cities, hiding in sewers and walls. Its sting can be dangerous to children.

name: Amazonian Giant Centipede
entry: It is the largest centipede in the world, over a foot long. In a cave in Venezuela, it was seen hanging from the ceiling and snatching bats out of the air.

name: Sally Lightfoot Crab
range: Pacific coast of South America & the Galápagos
entry: It is bright red and orange and races across wave-splashed rocks, even hopping from one to another. It can scuttle sideways, backward and forward with great speed.

name: Southern King Crab
range: Cold waters of southern Chile & Argentina
entry: Its leg span can reach three feet. It lives in the frigid channels of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. Despite its name, it is more closely related to hermit crabs than to true crabs.

name: Humboldt Squid
entry: It hunts in schools of up to 1,200 squid. It flashes red and white as it signals to others, earning it the name red devil. It can grow over five feet long and 100 pounds.

name: Channeled Apple Snail
range: Native to Argentina & Uruguay; invasive worldwide
entry: It lays clutches of bright pink eggs above the water line. The color warns predators that the eggs are toxic. It has a lung as well as a gill, and it eats so many plants that it is a pest in rice fields worldwide.

name: Giant Amazon Leech
entry: It is one of the largest leeches in the world, up to 18 inches long. Instead of jaws, it has a long, needle-like proboscis up to six inches long that it pushes into its host. Mothers carry their babies on their bellies.

name: Arapaima
entry: It is one of the largest freshwater fish, reaching ten feet long. It must come up to gulp air every 10 to 20 minutes. Its scales are so tough that piranhas cannot bite through them.

name: Red-bellied Piranha
range: Rivers of the Amazon & Paraná basins
entry: Its razor-sharp, interlocking teeth can slice through flesh and bone. Its fearsome reputation is exaggerated, though. It mostly scavenges, and it travels in schools for safety from larger predators.

name: Electric Eel
entry: It is not a true eel but a knifefish. Its body is lined with cells that work like batteries, and a close relative can release shocks of up to 860 volts, the strongest of any animal. It can leap out of the water to shock threats.

name: Candiru
entry: This tiny, see-through catfish slips into the gills of larger fish to drink their blood. Scary stories claim it swims into people, but almost none of these tales have ever been confirmed.

name: Four-eyed Fish
range: Coasts & mangroves of northern South America
entry: It has only two eyes, but each is split in half. It swims at the surface so the top half sees through the air while the bottom half sees underwater, watching for birds and fish at the same time.

name: Discus
entry: Both parents feed their babies with a special mucus that they produce on their skin, much like milk. The young cling to their parents' sides and nibble at it for their first weeks.

name: Neon Tetra
range: Blackwater streams of the upper Amazon
entry: A bright blue stripe runs along its side, glowing like a neon sign. The stripe may help schools stay together in dark water. It is one of the most popular aquarium fish in the world.

name: Splash Tetra
entry: A pair leaps out of the water together and sticks their eggs onto a leaf above the surface. The male stays below and splashes the eggs with his tail every few minutes to keep them wet until they hatch.

name: South American Lungfish
range: Swamps of the Amazon & Paraná basins
entry: It breathes air with a pair of lungs and will drown if kept underwater. In the dry season it digs into the mud and seals itself in a burrow. The male grows feathery gills on his fins that release oxygen for his eggs.

name: Ocellate River Stingray
entry: This freshwater stingray is covered in orange-ringed eyespots. It buries itself in sandy riverbeds, and its venomous tail spine can deliver a painful sting to people who step on it.

name: Red-lipped Batfish
range: Galápagos Islands & the coast of Peru
entry: It has bright red lips and walks along the sea floor on its stiff fins instead of swimming. A small lure on its head may help it catch prey. Scientists still debate why its lips are so red.

name: Paradoxical Frog Tadpole
entry: Its tadpole can grow up to nine inches long, one of the largest tadpoles of any frog. It spends months growing in ponds and swamps.

name: Paradoxical Frog
entry: When its giant tadpole changes into a frog, it shrinks to about a third of its tadpole length. This backward growth gave it its name.

name: Golden Poison Frog
entry: It may be the most poisonous animal on Earth, carrying enough toxin to kill ten grown men. The Emberá people coat their blowgun darts by rubbing them on its back. In captivity, fed a normal diet, it loses its poison.

name: Blue Poison Dart Frog
range: Forests of Suriname, French Guiana & Brazil
entry: Its brilliant blue skin, spotted with black, warns predators of its toxins. Each frog's spot pattern is unique. Fathers carry their tadpoles on their backs to small pools of water.

name: Cane Toad
range: Native to South & Central America; invasive in Australia
entry: Glands behind its eyes ooze a milky toxin that can kill dogs and native predators. It was brought to Australia in 1935 to eat beetles, but it spread across much of the continent instead.

name: Darwin's Frog
entry: The father picks up the developing eggs and keeps them in his vocal sac. The tadpoles grow there until they come out of his mouth as tiny froglets. Charles Darwin discovered it on his voyage.

name: Cranwell's Horned Frog
range: Gran Chaco of Argentina, Paraguay & Bolivia
entry: Its mouth is so large it can swallow animals nearly its own size, including other frogs and mice. It sits half-buried and ambushes whatever passes. It is often called the Pac-Man frog.

name: Amazon Milk Frog
entry: When threatened, it oozes a sticky white fluid that looks like milk and irritates predators. It lives high in the canopy and breeds in water-filled tree holes.

name: Green Anaconda
range: Swamps & rivers of the Amazon & Orinoco
entry: It is the heaviest snake in the world, with females weighing over 400 pounds. It waits in shallow water with only its eyes and nostrils showing, then grabs and squeezes prey as large as capybaras and caimans.

name: Black Caiman
entry: It is the largest predator in the Amazon, growing over 15 feet long. Its dark skin helps it hide in murky water at night. Overhunting for its leather nearly wiped it out, but it has recovered.

name: Galápagos Giant Tortoise
entry: It can live over 100 years. Islands with tall plants have tortoises with saddle-shaped shells that let them stretch their necks up high. Lonesome George, the last of his kind, died in 2012.

name: Marine Iguana
entry: It is the only lizard that swims in the ocean to feed, grazing on algae. It sneezes out extra salt through glands in its nose. In lean years, it can actually shrink its body, even its bones.

name: Galápagos Land Iguana
entry: Its yellow-orange body blends with the dry islands. It eats prickly pear cactus, spines and all, and gets most of its water that way. It can live over 60 years.

name: Mata Mata
entry: Its flat, bumpy shell and fringed head look like dead leaves on a riverbed. When a fish swims close, it opens its huge mouth in a flash and sucks the fish in like a vacuum.

name: Emerald Tree Boa
entry: It spends its life coiled over branches in the rainforest. Babies are born red or orange and turn emerald green as they grow. Heat-sensing pits along its lips help it find birds and bats at night.

name: Bushmaster
entry: It is the longest venomous snake in the Americas. Its scientific name means silent fate. It waits in ambush for weeks in the same spot, and unlike most vipers, it lays eggs.

name: Golden Lancehead
entry: It lives only on Queimada Grande, a small island off Brazil nicknamed Snake Island. With no mammals to eat, it hunts migrating birds and has one of the fastest-acting venoms of any lancehead. Visiting the island is banned.

name: Argentine Tegu
entry: During the breeding season, it can raise its body temperature above its surroundings, something almost no other reptile can do. It eats nearly anything, including eggs, fruit and small animals.

name: White Worm Lizard
entry: It looks like a giant worm, and its blunt tail looks like a second head. When threatened, it raises its tail as a decoy. It lives underground, often inside leafcutter ant nests, eating beetles.

name: Giant South American River Turtle
entry: It is the largest side-necked turtle. Thousands of females crawl onto the same sandbanks to nest together at night. Hatchlings call to each other from inside their eggs to hatch at the same time.

name: Hoatzin Chick
range: Swamps of the Amazon & Orinoco basins
entry: The chick has two claws on each wing, a feature that makes it look like a tiny dinosaur. When threatened, it drops into the water below its nest, then climbs back up using its wing claws.

name: Hoatzin
range: Swamps of the Amazon & Orinoco basins
entry: It eats almost nothing but leaves, which ferment in its oversized crop like in a cow's stomach. The fermenting leaves give it a smell like manure, earning it the name stinkbird. The adult loses its wing claws.

name: Andean Condor
entry: It is one of the heaviest flying birds, with a wingspan over ten feet. It rarely flaps, riding rising air for hours. One condor was recorded flying over 100 miles without a single wingbeat.

name: Harpy Eagle
entry: Its rear talons are longer than a grizzly bear's claws. It snatches sloths and monkeys from the treetops. The feathers on its face may help focus sound toward its ears.

name: Hyacinth Macaw
entry: It is the longest parrot in the world, with deep cobalt-blue feathers. Its huge beak can crack palm nuts so hard that people need a hammer to open them. It is threatened by the pet trade.

name: Scarlet Macaw
range: Rainforests from Mexico to the Amazon
entry: Flocks gather at riverbank cliffs to eat clay, which may give them salt or neutralize toxins in their diet of seeds. Pairs mate for life and can live over 40 years.

name: Sword-billed Hummingbird
entry: It is the only bird with a bill longer than its body. It feeds on flowers with extremely long tubes that no other bird can reach. To preen, it has to use its feet, and it perches with its bill pointed up.

name: Oilbird
entry: It is the only bird that flies at night to eat fruit, and it lives in caves. It finds its way in total darkness with clicking sounds, like a bat. Its screams in the caves sound eerie.

name: Andean Cock-of-the-rock
entry: Males have brilliant orange-red feathers and a crest that hides their bill. They gather to dance, bow and squawk to impress females. Females build mud nests on rock walls. It is the national bird of Peru.

name: Scarlet Ibis
range: Coasts of northern South America & Trinidad
entry: Its brilliant red color comes from pigments in the crabs and shrimp it eats. Young birds are gray-brown and slowly turn red. It is the national bird of Trinidad and Tobago.

name: Magellanic Penguin
range: Coasts of Argentina, Chile & the Falklands
entry: It nests in burrows along the coast of Patagonia, returning to the same burrow and partner year after year. It migrates north to Brazil in winter, swimming thousands of miles.

name: Flightless Cormorant
entry: It is the only cormorant that cannot fly. With no predators on its islands, its wings shrank to stubs, and it hunts by diving and swimming with powerful legs. It still spreads its tiny wings to dry them.

name: Medium Ground Finch
entry: Scientists watched its beaks grow larger in just a few years after a drought left only big, hard seeds to eat. Darwin's finches like it became a famous example of evolution happening fast enough to measure.

name: Waved Albatross
entry: Almost the whole population nests on a single Galápagos island. Pairs perform a long courtship dance of bill-fencing, bowing and clacking. It has a wingspan of about eight feet.

name: Greater Rhea
entry: It is the largest bird in the Americas. Several females lay eggs in one male's nest, and he alone sits on up to 50 eggs and guards the chicks, charging at anything that comes close.

name: Club-winged Manakin
entry: The male sings with his wings, not his voice. He rubs special feathers together over 100 times per second to make a violin-like ring. His wing bones are solid, unlike most birds'.

name: Horned Screamer
entry: A long, thin horn made of cartilage grows from its forehead. Each wing has two sharp spurs for fighting. Its loud honking calls can be heard miles away.

name: Inca Tern
range: Humboldt Current coasts of Peru & Chile
entry: It has dark gray feathers, a red bill and long white feathers that curl like a mustache. Healthier birds grow longer mustaches. It often steals scraps from sea lions and whales.

name: Toco Toucan
entry: It is the largest toucan, with an orange bill about a third of its body length. Scientists found that it controls blood flow to the bill to shed heat, like a radiator.

name: Giant Hummingbird
range: The Andes, from Ecuador to Chile
entry: It is the largest hummingbird in the world, about the size of a starling. In 2024, trackers revealed it is actually two species, and one flies about 5,000 miles to the high Andes and back.

name: Great Tinamou
entry: It lays glossy turquoise eggs that look like porcelain. The male sits on the eggs and raises the chicks alone. It can fly but prefers to walk quietly along the forest floor.

name: Rufous Hornero
entry: Pairs build a heavy nest of mud and straw shaped like a clay oven, with an inner chamber to keep out predators. It is the national bird of Argentina.

name: Capybara
entry: It is the largest rodent in the world. Its eyes, ears and nose sit on top of its head so it can hide underwater. It is so calm that birds, monkeys and other animals often sit on it.

name: Giant Anteater
entry: Its sticky tongue can flick in and out 150 times a minute to eat about 30,000 ants and termites a day. It walks on its knuckles to protect its long claws, which can fend off a jaguar.

name: Giant Armadillo
entry: It is the largest armadillo, with a middle claw up to eight inches long, one of the biggest claws of any animal. Its burrows are used as shelter by dozens of other species.

name: Amazon River Dolphin
entry: Adult males turn bright pink. Its neck bones are not fused, so it can turn its head to swim through flooded forests. Legends say it turns into a handsome man at night to charm people at parties.

name: Giant Otter
entry: It is the longest member of the weasel family, up to six feet. Family groups hunt fish together and will even drive off caimans. Each otter has a unique cream-colored throat patch.

name: Maned Wolf
entry: It looks like a fox on stilts, with long legs for seeing over tall grass. It is not a true wolf. Half its diet is fruit, especially the wolf apple, and its urine smells strongly like cannabis.

name: Spectacled Bear
entry: It is the only bear in South America. Pale markings around its eyes look like glasses, and each bear's pattern is unique. It builds platforms in trees to eat fruit. It inspired the story of Paddington Bear.

name: Vicuña
range: High Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Chile & Argentina
entry: It has one of the finest wools of any animal, which kept it warm at over 13,000 feet. Hunting nearly wiped it out, but today villagers round up wild vicuñas, shear them and release them.

name: Long-tailed Chinchilla
entry: It has the densest fur of any land animal, with up to 60 hairs growing from each pore. The fur is too thick for fleas to live in. It cleans itself by rolling in volcanic dust.

name: Pygmy Marmoset
entry: It is the smallest monkey in the world, weighing about as much as a stick of butter. It gnaws holes in tree bark and feeds on the gum and sap that ooze out.

name: Golden Lion Tamarin
entry: Its silky golden-orange mane makes it look like a tiny lion. By the 1970s only about 200 remained in the wild. Captive breeding and reforestation have brought it back to thousands.

name: Bearded Capuchin
entry: It cracks hard nuts by lifting heavy stones and slamming them down on rock anvils. Archaeologists have dug up capuchin stone tools at least 3,000 years old.

name: Greater Bulldog Bat
range: Coasts & rivers of Central & South America
entry: It skims over water at night and uses echolocation to detect the ripples of fish just below the surface. Then it rakes them up with its long, clawed feet.

name: White-lipped Peccary
entry: It roams in herds of hundreds, clacking its teeth loudly when threatened. A herd will defend itself against jaguars. It smells strongly from a scent gland on its back.

name: Southern Elephant Seal
range: Patagonia, the Falklands & the Southern Ocean
entry: Males can weigh over four tons and use their huge noses to make loud roars. It can dive over a mile deep and hold its breath for two hours. Males fight bloody battles for control of beaches.

name: Southern Pudu
entry: It is one of the smallest deer in the world, standing about 15 inches tall. It sometimes climbs fallen logs or bends saplings to reach leaves. When scared, it barks.

name: Patagonian Mara
entry: It looks like a mix of a rabbit and a small deer but is a rodent related to guinea pigs. Pairs stay together for life. Many pairs raise their young together in a shared burrow.

name: Monito del Monte
entry: This tiny marsupial is more closely related to Australian marsupials than to other South American ones. It stores fat in its tail and hibernates through winter. It is the only animal that spreads the seeds of a local mistletoe.

name: Bald Uakari
range: Flooded forests of the western Amazon
entry: Its bald face is bright red, and a redder face means a healthier monkey. Pale-faced uakaris may be sick with malaria. It uses strong teeth to crack open unripe fruits.

name: Brazilian Porcupine
range: Forests of northern & central South America
entry: It lives in trees and grips branches with a long tail. Its short, sharp quills come loose easily and hook into attackers. It is active at night and eats leaves, fruit and seeds.

name: Kinkajou
entry: It is related to raccoons but hangs from branches by its tail like a monkey. Its five-inch tongue reaches nectar and honey, earning it the name honey bear. It can turn its feet backward to run down trees.

name: Bush Dog
entry: This short-legged wild dog has webbed feet and is an excellent swimmer. Packs chase prey into the water and hunt animals much larger than themselves, like capybaras.

name: Andean Mountain Cat
range: High Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Chile & Argentina
entry: It is one of the rarest cats in the world, living above 13,000 feet. Its long, thick tail helps it balance on rocky slopes. Andean peoples consider it sacred.

name: South American Coati
entry: It uses its long, flexible snout to sniff out insects and spiders in leaf litter. Females and young travel in noisy groups of up to 30, holding their striped tails high.

name: Lowland Tapir
entry: It is the largest land mammal in South America. It spreads the seeds of many trees in its droppings, earning it the nickname gardener of the forest. It swims well and hides underwater.

name: Linnaeus's Two-toed Sloth
entry: It spends almost its whole life hanging upside down, even eating and sleeping. Its fur grows from belly to back so rain runs off while it hangs. It can take a month to digest a meal.

name: Southern Right Whale
range: Southern Ocean; calves off Península Valdés, Argentina
entry: Rough, pale patches called callosities grow on its head, and each whale's pattern is unique. It sometimes holds its tail up in the wind like a sail. Whalers called it the right whale to hunt because it floated when killed.

name: Pink Fairy Armadillo
entry: It is the smallest armadillo, about the size of a stick of butter. Its pink shell is attached only along its back, and it swims through sand using huge front claws. A flat plate on its rear plugs its burrow.

name: Corpse Lily
entry: It makes the largest single flower on Earth, up to three feet across and about 24 pounds. It has no leaves, stems or roots of its own and lives hidden inside a jungle vine. The bloom smells like rotting meat to attract carrion flies.

name: Titan Arum
entry: Its flower spike can tower over ten feet high. When it blooms, the spike heats itself to near human body temperature, helping spread a smell of rotting meat. It may bloom only once every several years.

name: Rajah Pitcher Plant
entry: Its pitchers can hold over two quarts of fluid and have been found with drowned rats inside. More often, tree shrews visit to lick nectar from the lid and leave their droppings in the pitcher, which feeds the plant.

name: Sacred Lotus
entry: A lotus seed found in a dry lakebed in China sprouted after about 1,300 years. Its flowers can warm themselves to around 95°F even on cool days. It is a holy symbol of purity in Hinduism and Buddhism.

name: Ginkgo
entry: It is the last survivor of a group of trees that thrived alongside the dinosaurs. Several ginkgos in Hiroshima survived the 1945 atomic bomb and are still alive. Female trees drop seeds that smell like rancid butter.

name: Moso Bamboo
entry: It is one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth and can grow over three feet in a single day. Whole forests flower at the same time, only once every several decades, and then die.

name: Edelweiss
range: The Alps & other mountains of Europe
entry: Its star-shaped flowers are covered in thick white wool that shields them from cold, wind and strong mountain sunlight. It grows on high rocky slopes and became a symbol of the Alps.

name: Opium Poppy
entry: Its unripe seed pods ooze a milky sap containing morphine and codeine, some of medicine's most important painkillers. The same sap has fueled centuries of addiction and even wars.

name: Deadly Nightshade
entry: Its shiny black berries taste sweet but are deadly. Belladonna means beautiful lady, because women in Renaissance Italy used its juice to widen their pupils. Doctors still use its chemical, atropine.

name: Mandrake
entry: Its thick, forked root can look like a tiny human. Old legends claimed it screamed when pulled up and killed anyone who heard it. The whole plant is poisonous and can cause hallucinations.

name: Stinging Nettle
entry: Its leaves and stems are covered in hollow hairs tipped with silica, like tiny glass needles. They snap off in skin and inject chemicals that burn and itch. Cooked, the leaves are safe to eat.

name: Tea Plant
entry: Every true tea, from green to black to oolong, comes from this one plant. The difference is in how the leaves are processed. Left unpruned, it can grow into a tree over 30 feet tall.

name: European Mistletoe
entry: It grows on tree branches and steals their water. Birds eat its white berries and wipe the sticky seeds onto new branches. Druids considered it sacred, and people still kiss beneath it at Christmas.

name: Dahurian Larch
entry: It is the northernmost tree on Earth and survives winters colder than -70°F. Unlike most conifers, it drops all its needles each autumn. It forms vast forests over permanently frozen ground.

name: Dragon's Blood Tree
entry: Its dense, umbrella-shaped crown shades its roots and catches moisture from mist. When the bark is cut, it bleeds a dark red resin that was once sold as dragon's blood for dyes and medicine.

name: Sphagnum Moss
entry: It can hold about 20 times its dry weight in water. It makes its bog so acidic and airless that decay nearly stops, and human bodies over 2,000 years old have been found preserved in peat.

name: Durian
entry: Its fruit is covered in sharp spikes and can weigh up to seven pounds. The smell is so strong that it is banned on many buses, trains and hotels in Southeast Asia, yet fans call it the king of fruits.

name: Caterpillar Fungus
entry: It infects ghost moth caterpillars underground, kills them and sprouts a stalk out of their heads. It is prized in traditional medicine and can sell for more than its weight in gold.

name: Black Truffle
entry: It grows underground on the roots of oak and hazel trees. To spread its spores, it gives off a strong scent that draws animals to dig it up. Trained dogs and pigs sniff it out, and it can sell for over $1,000 a pound.

name: Night-light Mushroom
entry: This tiny mushroom glows a soft green in the dark, especially after rain. Its light may attract insects that help spread its spores. In Japan it is called yakoutake, the night-light mushroom.

name: Death Cap
entry: It causes most deaths from mushroom poisoning worldwide. Half a cap can kill an adult, and cooking does not destroy the toxin. Symptoms often ease after a day or two, even as the poison keeps destroying the liver.

name: Reindeer Lichen
range: Arctic tundra & taiga of Europe & Asia
entry: It forms spongy gray carpets across the tundra and grows only a few millimeters a year. It is the main winter food of reindeer, which dig through the snow to reach it.

name: Many-headed Slime Mold
range: Damp forests of Europe, Asia & beyond
entry: It is a single giant cell with many nuclei. When scientists placed oat flakes in the pattern of cities around Tokyo, it grew a network of tubes strikingly similar to the real Tokyo rail system.

name: Silkworm
range: Domesticated in China; no wild populations
entry: It eats only mulberry leaves and spins its cocoon from a single silk thread up to a mile long. People in China have raised it for over 5,000 years, and it no longer lives in the wild.

name: Domestic Silk Moth
range: Domesticated in China; no wild populations
entry: After thousands of years of breeding, it can no longer fly and depends completely on people. The adult has no working mouth and lives only a few days, long enough to mate and lay eggs.

name: Emperor Dragonfly Nymph
entry: It lives underwater for up to two years. It snatches tadpoles and small fish with a folding lower lip that shoots out like an arm, and it escapes danger by squirting water out of its rear.

name: Emperor Dragonfly
entry: It is one of Europe's largest dragonflies. It spends most of the day on the wing, hunting and even eating in flight. Males patrol their ponds and chase off any rival.

name: Antlion Larva
entry: It digs a cone-shaped pit in loose sand and waits buried at the bottom. When an ant slips in, it flicks sand to knock it down, then grabs it with its sickle-shaped jaws.

name: Antlion
entry: After two or three years in the sand, the larva becomes a delicate winged adult that looks like a damselfly. It flutters weakly at night and lives only a few weeks.

name: Asian Giant Hornet
entry: It is the largest hornet in the world, up to two inches long. A small group can wipe out a hive of 30,000 European honey bees in a few hours, biting off their heads.

name: Japanese Honey Bee
entry: When a giant hornet scout enters the hive, hundreds of bees swarm it into a tight ball and vibrate their flight muscles. The ball heats to about 115°F and cooks the hornet alive, a temperature the bees can survive.

name: Orchid Mantis
entry: Its pink and white body and petal-shaped legs make it look like a flower. Insects find it even more attractive than real flowers, and it grabs them when they come close.

name: Atlas Moth
entry: It is one of the largest moths in the world, with wings nearly a foot across. The tips of its forewings look like snake heads. The adult has no mouth and lives only about a week.

name: Japanese Rhinoceros Beetle
entry: Males use their forked horns to flip rivals off tree branches in battles over sap. In Japan it is called kabutomushi, and children keep it as a pet and hold beetle wrestling matches.

name: Synchronous Firefly
range: Mangroves of Malaysia, Thailand & the Philippines
entry: Thousands of males gather in riverside mangrove trees and flash their lights in perfect unison. Whole trees blink on and off together like holiday lights, drawing in females from far away.

name: Violin Beetle
entry: Its body is so flat and wide that it looks like a violin. The shape lets it slip between layers of shelf fungi. When attacked, it sprays an acid that can numb skin.

name: Chan's Megastick
entry: It is one of the longest insects in the world, over 22 inches with its legs stretched out. It hangs motionless in the treetops looking like a twig. Its eggs have wing-like flaps that help them drift on the wind.

name: Emerald Cockroach Wasp
range: South & Southeast Asia, Africa & Pacific islands
entry: It stings a cockroach twice, the second time directly into its brain, turning it into an obedient zombie. The wasp leads it by an antenna like a dog on a leash to a burrow, where its larva eats the roach alive.

name: Weaver Ant
entry: Workers form living chains to pull leaves together, then weave them into nests with silk from their own larvae. Farmers in China have used these ants to protect citrus trees from pests for over 1,700 years.

name: Exploding Ant
entry: When an enemy attacks, a worker squeezes its body until it bursts, spraying sticky, toxic yellow goo on the attacker. It sacrifices itself to protect the colony.

name: Mountain Apollo
entry: This white butterfly with red eyespots lives in high mountain meadows. It warms up on cold mornings by basking its dark body in the sun. It is declining as its mountains grow warmer.

name: Rajah Brooke's Birdwing
entry: Its black wings carry bright green bands shaped like feathers. It is named after James Brooke, the first White Rajah of Sarawak. Males gather in groups on riverbanks to drink minerals from damp soil.

name: Orange Oakleaf
entry: With its wings closed, it looks exactly like a dry, dead leaf, complete with a midrib and veins. When it opens its wings, it flashes bright blue and orange.

name: Death's-head Hawkmoth
entry: It has a skull-like pattern on its back. It sneaks into beehives to steal honey, likely using a scent that mimics the bees. When handled, it lets out a loud squeak.

name: European Mole Cricket
entry: Its front legs are shaped like a mole's shovels. Males dig burrows shaped like a horn, which makes their songs louder and carry farther.

name: Lantern Bug
entry: It has a long red snout that early naturalists wrongly believed glowed at night like a lantern. It actually uses the snout to drink tree sap, especially from longan trees.

name: Giant Golden Orb-weaver
entry: Its huge webs, over three feet across, are woven from golden silk that shines in sunlight. The female can be more than ten times bigger than the male.

name: Segmented Trapdoor Spider
entry: It belongs to the most ancient living group of spiders and still has segmented plates on its abdomen like its ancestors. It hides in a burrow under a trapdoor and senses prey through silk trip lines.

name: Portia Jumping Spider
entry: It hunts other spiders by plucking their webs to imitate a trapped insect. It can plan long, roundabout routes to sneak up on prey, even when it loses sight of the prey along the way.

name: Varroa Mite
range: Native to East Asia; now worldwide
entry: It clings to honey bees and feeds on their fat. It jumped from Asian honey bees to European honey bees and is now one of the biggest threats to beekeeping worldwide.

name: House Centipede
range: Native to the Mediterranean; now worldwide
entry: It has 15 pairs of long legs and can run over a foot per second. If a predator grabs a leg, it drops it and keeps running. It hunts cockroaches, silverfish and other pests in houses.

name: Japanese Spider Crab
entry: It has the longest legs of any arthropod, spanning up to 12 feet from claw to claw. It may live up to 100 years. It decorates its shell with sponges and other animals for camouflage.

name: Chinese Mitten Crab
range: Native to East Asia; invasive in Europe
entry: Its claws are covered in thick brown hair, like mittens. It lives in rivers but walks to the sea to breed. It has spread to Europe and North America, where it clogs pipes and damages riverbanks.

name: Chambered Nautilus
range: Deep reefs of the Philippines & Indo-Pacific
entry: Its shell is divided into chambers, and it controls its depth by adjusting the gas and liquid inside them, like a submarine. Nautiluses have swum the oceans for about 500 million years. It has up to 90 tentacles and no suckers.

name: Sea Bunny
range: Coasts of Japan & the western Pacific
entry: This tiny sea slug looks like a fluffy white rabbit. Its ears are rhinophores used to smell, and its fur is made of tiny rods covering its body. It became an internet sensation in Japan.

name: Mimic Octopus
entry: It impersonates other animals to scare off predators, spreading its arms like a lionfish, flattening itself like a flounder, or waving two arms like a banded sea snake. It was only discovered in 1998.

name: Greater Blue-ringed Octopus
range: Tropical western Pacific, including Japan & the Philippines
entry: When threatened, dozens of bright blue rings flash across its body. Its saliva carries tetrodotoxin, enough to kill several adults, and there is no antivenom.

name: Nomura's Jellyfish
entry: It is one of the largest jellyfish in the world, up to 6.5 feet across and 440 pounds. In some years huge swarms drift into Japanese waters, crushing fishing nets and even capsizing a trawler.

name: Immortal Jellyfish
entry: When injured or starving, it can turn back into a young polyp and start life over. In theory it can repeat this again and again, which makes it biologically immortal.

name: Medicinal Leech
entry: It has three jaws with about 100 teeth each and leaves a Y-shaped bite. Its saliva numbs the skin and keeps blood from clotting. Surgeons still use it to restore blood flow after reattaching fingers and ears.

name: Bobbit Worm
entry: It buries its long body, which can be several feet, in the sea floor and waits with its jaws open. When a fish swims close, it strikes so fast it can slice the fish in half, then drags it into its burrow.

name: Common Earthworm
entry: It breathes through its skin and pulls fallen leaves down into its burrow at night. Charles Darwin studied it for decades and wrote his final book about how worms build soil.

name: Venus' Flower Basket
range: Deep western Pacific, including Japan & the Philippines
entry: Its skeleton is a delicate lattice of glass. A pair of shrimp often enter it while young, grow too big to leave, and spend their whole lives inside. In Japan it has been given as a wedding gift symbolizing lifelong love.

name: Leptocephalus
range: The Sargasso Sea to Europe's coasts
entry: The European eel hatches in the Sargasso Sea as a clear, leaf-shaped larva. It drifts on ocean currents toward Europe for months or even years.

name: Glass Eel
entry: Nearing the coast, it changes into a see-through miniature eel. Millions swim up European rivers each spring. Glass eels are so valuable that they are smuggled to Asian eel farms.

name: European Eel
entry: It can live in rivers and ponds for decades. Then it turns silver, swims thousands of miles back to the Sargasso Sea to spawn once, and dies. Its numbers have crashed, and it is now critically endangered.

name: Beluga Sturgeon
entry: It is one of the largest freshwater fish ever recorded, with some over 20 feet long. Its eggs are sold as beluga caviar, the most expensive kind. Overfishing has made it critically endangered.

name: Koi
range: Bred in Japan from wild carp of East Asia
entry: Koi were bred in Japan from wild carp for their colors. A Chinese legend says a carp that leaps over the Dragon Gate waterfall becomes a dragon. A famous koi named Hanako was said to have lived 226 years.

name: Banded Archerfish
entry: It knocks insects off leaves by shooting jets of water from its mouth, correcting its aim for how light bends at the surface. In experiments, archerfish learned to recognize human faces.

name: Siamese Fighting Fish
entry: Males flare their fins and gill covers and fight fiercely over territory. They breathe air from the surface, so they survive in small, warm puddles. The male builds a nest of bubbles for his eggs.

name: Frilled Shark
range: Deep waters worldwide; often seen off Japan
entry: It looks like an ancient sea serpent, with a long, eel-like body and about 300 needle-shaped teeth in 25 rows. Its pregnancy may last over three years, the longest known of any animal.

name: Goblin Shark
range: Deep waters worldwide; most often off Japan
entry: When it bites, its jaws shoot forward out of its mouth like a slingshot to snatch prey. It lives in the deep sea and is rarely seen alive. Its pink color comes from blood vessels showing through its skin.

name: Mandarinfish
entry: It is one of the very few animals colored blue by pigment rather than by light-bending structures. It has no scales and is coated in smelly, toxic mucus. Pairs rise together at dusk to spawn.

name: Barreleye
range: Deep North Pacific, including off Japan
entry: Its head is covered by a clear, fluid-filled shield. Its green eyes sit inside and can rotate to look straight up or forward through its see-through head. The two spots above its mouth are nostrils, not eyes.

name: Climbing Perch
entry: A special breathing organ lets it survive out of water. During droughts, it can wriggle across land from one pond to another using its gill covers and fins.

name: Common Frog Tadpole
entry: It hatches from a clump of jelly-coated eggs in early spring. It breathes through gills and grazes on algae, growing legs as it turns into a frog over about three months.

name: Common Frog
entry: It is one of Europe's most widespread frogs and lives even above the Arctic Circle. Males gather in ponds in early spring and grab females in a hug that can last for days.

name: Olm
range: Caves of the Dinaric Alps, from Slovenia to Bosnia
entry: When floods washed olms out of caves, people in Slovenia believed they were baby dragons. It is blind, can live over 100 years, and can survive up to ten years without eating.

name: Fire Salamander
entry: Medieval Europeans believed it could survive fire, because salamanders fled out of burning logs. Its black and yellow skin warns of a toxin it can spray. Mothers give birth to live larvae in streams.

name: Wallace's Flying Frog
entry: It glides from tree to tree using huge webbed feet as parachutes, traveling up to 50 feet. It was described by Alfred Russel Wallace, who came up with the theory of evolution by natural selection at the same time as Darwin.

name: Common Midwife Toad
entry: The father wraps strings of eggs around his hind legs and carries them for weeks, keeping them moist. When they are ready to hatch, he wades into a pond to release the tadpoles.

name: Komodo Dragon
entry: It is the largest living lizard, up to ten feet long. Its bite delivers venom that keeps blood from clotting. Females can lay eggs that hatch without any male.

name: King Cobra
entry: It is the longest venomous snake, reaching over 18 feet, and it eats mostly other snakes. It is the only snake that builds a nest, raking leaves into a mound for its eggs. It can rear up to look a person in the eye.

name: Gharial
entry: Its long, thin snout is lined with over 100 sharp teeth, perfect for snapping at fish. Adult males grow a bulb on the tip of the snout, called a ghara after an Indian pot, which they use to make buzzing sounds.

name: Saltwater Crocodile
range: Coasts of India, Southeast Asia & northern Australia
entry: It is the largest living reptile, with males over 20 feet long. It has the strongest bite ever measured in a living animal. It can ride ocean currents for hundreds of miles between islands.

name: Common Flying Dragon
entry: It spreads flaps of skin supported by long ribs to glide between trees, traveling 30 feet or more. Males flash a bright yellow throat flag to warn rivals.

name: Tokay Gecko
