entry: Its loud call sounds like to-kay, which gave it its name. It bites hard and holds on. Millions of tiny hairs on its toes let it run up glass and cling upside down.

name: Reticulated Python
entry: It is the longest snake in the world, with record lengths over 20 feet. Its net-like pattern breaks up its outline on the forest floor. It swims well and has colonized many small islands.

name: Paradise Tree Snake
entry: It launches from branches, flattens its body and slithers through the air, gliding over 30 yards. Its mild venom is harmless to people but helps it catch lizards and bats.

name: Big-headed Turtle
range: Mountain streams of southern China & Southeast Asia
entry: Its head is too big to pull into its shell, so it is armored with a bony shield instead. It climbs over rocks and even into low trees using its claws and tail.

name: Slow Worm
entry: It looks like a snake but is a legless lizard that can blink and drop its tail. One slow worm in a zoo lived to be 54 years old.

name: Common Kingfisher
entry: It dives into water to catch fish with barely a splash. Japanese engineers modeled the nose of the 500 Series bullet train on its beak, making the train quieter and faster.

name: Mandarin Duck
entry: The male has orange, sail-shaped feathers on his back and a riot of other colors. Pairs are a symbol of love and loyalty in China. Ducklings leap from tree-hole nests high above the ground.

name: Eurasian Eagle-owl
entry: It is one of the largest owls in the world, with a wingspan over six feet. It can take prey as big as young deer and even other owls and hawks. Its deep hoot carries for miles.

name: Common Cuckoo
entry: It lays its eggs in other birds' nests, matching the color of the host's eggs. The newly hatched cuckoo pushes the host's eggs out of the nest. Its two-note call gave it its name and inspired the cuckoo clock.

name: Steller's Sea Eagle
entry: It is the heaviest eagle in the world, with a huge orange beak. In winter, large numbers gather on the sea ice off Hokkaido, Japan, to catch fish.

name: Himalayan Monal
range: The Himalayas, from Afghanistan to Bhutan
entry: The male's feathers shimmer in metallic green, blue, purple and copper. It lives high in the mountains and digs up roots and insects with its strong bill. It is the national bird of Nepal.

name: Bar-headed Goose
range: Central Asia; migrates over the Himalayas
entry: It migrates over the Himalayas, flying as high as 23,000 feet, where the air has about a third as much oxygen as at sea level. Its blood grabs oxygen much better than that of most birds.

name: Red-crowned Crane
entry: Pairs dance together in the snow, leaping, bowing and calling in unison. It is a symbol of luck and long life in Japan and China. Legend says folding 1,000 paper cranes grants a wish.

name: Great Hornbill
entry: The female seals herself inside a tree hollow with mud and droppings, leaving only a narrow slit. The male feeds her and the chick through the slit for months. Its huge yellow casque sits on top of its bill.

name: Common Swift
range: Breeds in Europe & Asia; winters in Africa
entry: After leaving the nest, it can stay in the air for ten months without landing, eating, drinking and even sleeping on the wing. A swift may fly millions of miles in its lifetime.

name: Common Starling
entry: On winter evenings, huge flocks swirl through the sky in shifting shapes called murmurations. Each bird tracks its seven nearest neighbors, so the whole flock moves as one. It is also a skilled mimic.

name: Eurasian Magpie
entry: It was the first non-mammal shown to recognize itself in a mirror, trying to remove a mark placed on its own feathers. It is bold and clever, though its reputation for stealing shiny things is mostly a myth.

name: Eurasian Hoopoe
entry: It fans out a striking crest of orange feathers like a crown. Nesting females and chicks coat themselves in a foul-smelling oil, and chicks can squirt feces at intruders. It is the national bird of Israel.

name: Indian Peafowl
entry: The male fans a train of over 100 shimmering eyespots and shakes it to make a rattling sound. Females often choose males with the most impressive trains. It is the national bird of India.

name: Philippine Eagle
entry: It is one of the largest and most powerful eagles, with a shaggy crest. It hunts colugos and monkeys in the forest canopy. A pair raises only one chick every two years, and only a few hundred pairs remain.

name: Wallcreeper
entry: It climbs sheer cliff faces in little hops, flicking open its crimson wings like a butterfly. It uses its long, thin bill to pick insects out of cracks in the rock.

name: Giant Panda
entry: It eats almost nothing but bamboo, up to 40 pounds a day. An enlarged wrist bone works like a thumb to grip stalks. Once endangered, its numbers have grown, and it is now listed as vulnerable.

name: Red Panda
entry: It is not a bear or a raccoon but the only living member of its own family. Like the giant panda, it eats bamboo and has a false thumb. One of its nicknames, firefox, inspired the name of a web browser.

name: Siberian Tiger
entry: It is one of the largest cats in the world. Thick fur and a layer of fat protect it from winters of -40°F. A tiger's stripes are on its skin as well as its fur, and every pattern is unique.

name: Snow Leopard
entry: It is so rarely seen that it is called the ghost of the mountains. Its thick tail is nearly as long as its body, helping it balance on cliffs and serving as a scarf when it sleeps. Unlike other big cats, it cannot roar.

name: Asian Elephant
entry: It is one of the few animals known to recognize itself in a mirror. It is smaller than the African elephant, with smaller ears. Only some males grow tusks.

name: Bornean Orangutan
entry: Its name means person of the forest in Malay. It builds a fresh nest of branches to sleep in every night. Young orangutans stay with their mothers for about eight years, longer than any animal besides humans.

name: Proboscis Monkey
entry: Males have huge, drooping noses that make their honking calls louder, and females prefer males with bigger noses. It is an excellent swimmer, with partly webbed feet.

name: Japanese Macaque
entry: It lives farther north than any other monkey besides humans. In the snowy mountains of Nagano, some troops soak in hot springs to keep warm. One group learned to wash sweet potatoes in the sea, and the habit spread through the troop.

name: Philippine Tarsier
entry: Each of its eyes is as big as its whole brain. Its eyes cannot move, so it turns its head nearly all the way around instead. It calls to others in ultrasound too high for humans to hear.

name: Sunda Slow Loris
entry: It is the only venomous primate. It licks a gland on its elbow and mixes the oil with saliva to make its bite toxic. It moves slowly and silently through the trees at night.

name: Sunda Colugo
entry: It is not a lemur and cannot truly fly, but it glides over 300 feet on a skin membrane that stretches from its neck to the tip of its tail. Colugos are among the closest living relatives of primates.

name: Malayan Tapir
entry: Its black-and-white coat breaks up its shape in moonlit forests. It grabs leaves with its short, flexible snout. Babies are born with stripes and spots like a watermelon, which fade within months.

name: Bactrian Camel
entry: Its two humps store fat, not water. It can gulp down about 30 gallons of water in minutes. Its thick winter coat helps it survive temperatures from -40°F to over 100°F.

name: Saiga
entry: Its large, floppy nose filters dust in summer and warms cold air in winter. In 2015 a bacterial disease killed over 200,000 saiga, more than half the population, in a few weeks. Its numbers have since recovered well.

name: Przewalski's Horse
entry: It vanished from the wild in the 1960s and survived only in zoos. Every living one descends from about a dozen horses. Since 1992 it has been returned to the steppes of Mongolia.

name: Wild Yak
entry: It lives higher than almost any other large mammal, up to 20,000 feet. Its shaggy coat hangs nearly to the ground, and it has large lungs for the thin air. Wild yaks are much bigger than domestic ones.

name: Reindeer
entry: Its eyes change from gold in summer to deep blue in winter, which helps it see in the long Arctic darkness. It is the only deer in which both males and females grow antlers. Its knees click as it walks.

name: European Hedgehog
entry: It has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines and rolls into a prickly ball when threatened. It sometimes licks strong-smelling things and smears foamy spit onto its spines, a behavior called self-anointing.

name: European Mole
entry: It can dig dozens of feet of tunnel in a day. It bites earthworms to paralyze them and stores hundreds in underground larders to eat later.

name: Syrian Hamster
entry: Nearly all pet Syrian hamsters descend from a single litter dug up near Aleppo in 1930. Its cheek pouches stretch back to its shoulders to carry food home. In the wild it is now endangered.

name: Etruscan Shrew
entry: It is the smallest mammal by weight, less than a tenth of an ounce. Its heart can beat over 1,500 times a minute, and it must eat about twice its own weight every day to stay alive.

name: Baikal Seal
entry: It is the only seal that lives only in fresh water, in Lake Baikal, the deepest lake on Earth. It keeps breathing holes open in the winter ice with its claws. How its ancestors reached the lake is still a mystery.

name: Binturong
entry: Its scent markings smell like buttered popcorn, thanks to the same chemical that gives popcorn its aroma. It is neither a bear nor a cat, and it is one of only two carnivores with a grasping tail.

name: Pallas's Cat
entry: It has the densest fur of any cat, which makes it look round and grumpy. Its pupils stay round instead of narrowing into slits. It is a slow runner and survives by hiding among rocks.

name: North Sulawesi Babirusa
entry: The male's upper tusks grow straight up through the top of his snout and curve back toward his forehead. If they are not worn down, they can grow into the skull. Its name means pig-deer in Malay.

name: Baobab
entry: Its swollen trunk can store thousands of gallons of water for the dry season. Some baobabs have lived more than 2,000 years. Its big white flowers open at night and are pollinated by fruit bats.

name: Welwitschia
entry: It grows only two leaves in its entire life. They keep growing from the base for centuries, splitting into ribbons as the desert wind shreds them. Some plants are thought to be over 1,500 years old.

name: Quiver Tree
entry: San hunters hollowed out its branches to make quivers for their arrows. In extreme heat, a tree may seal off and drop whole branches so the rest of it can survive.

name: Living Stones
entry: It looks just like a pebble, which keeps thirsty animals from eating it. Most of the plant sits underground, and sunlight reaches the inside through a clear window on top of each leaf.

name: King Protea
entry: It has one of the largest flower heads of any plant, up to a foot across. After wildfires sweep the fynbos, it sprouts again from a thick underground stem. It is South Africa's national flower.

name: Bird of Paradise Flower
entry: Its flower looks like a bright bird's head. When a sunbird lands on the blue petals to drink nectar, the petals open under its weight and dust its feet with pollen.

name: Rosy Periwinkle
entry: Compounds from this small flower, vincristine and vinblastine, became key drugs for treating childhood leukemia and other cancers. The whole plant is poisonous if eaten.

name: Arabica Coffee
entry: Its seeds are packed with caffeine, which protects them from insects. Wild coffee still grows in the forests of Ethiopia, where people first began brewing it. Legend says a goat herder noticed his goats dancing after eating the berries.

name: Jackal Food
entry: It has no leaves and no chlorophyll, and it lives underground feeding on the roots of euphorbia plants. Only its fleshy flower pokes out of the sand, giving off a smell of dung that lures beetles inside.

name: Wood's Cycad
range: Extinct in the wild; once Ngoye Forest, South Africa
entry: Only one wild plant was ever found, a male, in 1895. Every Wood's cycad alive today is a clone of that one plant. No female has ever been found, so it cannot reproduce naturally.

name: Cape Sundew
entry: Its leaves glisten with sticky droplets that look like nectar. When an insect gets stuck, the whole leaf slowly curls around it and digests it.

name: Mother of Thousands
entry: Tiny baby plants grow in rows along the edges of its leaves, then drop off and root wherever they land. It is toxic to animals that eat it and spreads so easily that it is invasive in many countries.

name: Whistling Thorn
entry: Ants live inside its swollen thorns and swarm out to bite giraffes and elephants that try to eat it. When the ants chew exit holes, wind blowing across them makes the tree whistle.

name: Sausage Tree
entry: Its fruit can grow two feet long and weigh up to 20 pounds, hanging from long stalks like sausages. Its dark red flowers open at night and are pollinated by bats.

name: Carrion Flower
entry: Its huge star-shaped flower can be over a foot wide and smells like rotting meat. Flies are fooled into laying eggs on it and carry its pollen away.

name: Papyrus
range: The Nile Valley & wetlands of tropical Africa
entry: Ancient Egyptians sliced its pith into strips, pressed them together and made one of the first kinds of paper. Floating mats of papyrus can form islands in East African lakes.

name: Giant Groundsel
entry: It lives high on Kilimanjaro, where nights freeze and days are hot. Each night its rosette of leaves folds in over the bud like a blanket. Dead leaves stay on the trunk as insulation.

name: Giant Lobelia
entry: Its rosette holds a pool of water that freezes over at night. The layer of ice protects the bud underneath from the much colder air above.

name: Termite Mushroom
entry: It is one of the biggest mushrooms in the world, with a cap that can reach three feet across. It grows only from termite mounds, where termites farm the fungus underground on chewed plant matter.

name: Veiled Lady
entry: It pushes up from the soil and unfurls a lacy white skirt in just a few hours. Its cap is coated in smelly, sticky slime that attracts flies, which carry off its spores.

name: Namib Fog Lichen
entry: It forms orange tufts across the gravel plains of the Namib Desert, where rain almost never falls. It survives by soaking up water from the fog that rolls in from the cold Atlantic.

name: Citrus Swallowtail Caterpillar
entry: When young, it looks exactly like a bird dropping, so birds ignore it. As it grows it turns green to match citrus leaves, and it flicks out a smelly orange organ when disturbed.

name: Citrus Swallowtail
entry: A strong, fast flyer, it is one of the most common swallowtails in Africa. Unlike many swallowtails it has no tails. Its caterpillars feed on orange and lemon trees, so farmers treat it as a pest.

name: Mopane Worm
entry: This big, spiky caterpillar feeds on mopane tree leaves. Millions are harvested every year, squeezed, dried and eaten as a protein-rich food across southern Africa.

name: Mopane Emperor Moth
entry: Large eyespots on its hindwings startle predators. The adult has no working mouth and lives only a few days, just long enough to find a mate and lay eggs.

name: Desert Locust (Solitary)
range: The Sahara, the Sahel & the Middle East
entry: Most of the time it is a shy, well-camouflaged grasshopper that avoids others of its kind. But when rain brings plenty of food and crowds form, being bumped on the hind legs triggers a dramatic change.

name: Desert Locust (Swarm)
range: The Sahara, the Sahel & the Middle East
entry: In its swarm phase it turns yellow and black and seeks out other locusts. Swarms can hold billions of insects and travel over 80 miles a day. A single square mile of swarm eats as much food in a day as tens of thousands of people.

name: Mocker Swallowtail
entry: Males look alike everywhere, but females come in many different color forms. Each form copies a different toxic butterfly from its area, so birds leave it alone. Scientists have studied it for over a century to learn how mimicry evolves.

name: Goliath Beetle
range: Tropical forests of Central & West Africa
entry: It is one of the heaviest insects in the world. Males use a Y-shaped horn to battle over food and mates. Despite its size it flies well, with a loud buzz like a small helicopter.

name: Namib Desert Beetle
entry: On foggy mornings it climbs to the top of a dune and does a headstand into the wind. Fog condenses on its back and trickles down into its mouth.

name: Sacred Scarab
entry: It rolls balls of dung in a straight line to escape rivals. Ancient Egyptians saw in it the god Khepri, who rolled the sun across the sky. Some African dung beetles steer at night by the glow of the Milky Way.

name: Driver Ant
entry: Colonies can hold over 20 million ants, among the largest of any ant. Blind workers pour through the forest in raids, eating any small animal that cannot get away. Their jaws grip so tightly that people have used them to stitch wounds.

name: African Honey Bee
entry: It defends its hive far more fiercely than European honey bees and will chase a threat for hundreds of feet. Elephants avoid its hives, so farmers now hang hives along fences to keep elephants out of their crops.

name: Tsetse Fly
entry: It feeds only on blood and spreads the parasite that causes sleeping sickness. Instead of laying eggs, the female grows one larva at a time inside her body and feeds it a kind of milk.

name: African Malaria Mosquito
entry: The female needs blood to make her eggs, and she can carry the parasite that causes malaria. It prefers to bite humans over other animals, which makes it one of the deadliest animals on Earth.

name: Mound-building Termite
entry: Its colony builds towering mounds of mud that can reach over 20 feet high. Tunnels inside act like lungs, moving air to keep the nest comfortable. Deep inside, the termites grow a fungus garden for food.

name: Devil's Flower Mantis
entry: It is one of the largest mantises in the world. It hangs upside down looking like a flower. When threatened, it rears up and flashes the red, white and blue on its front legs.

name: Madagascar Hissing Cockroach
entry: It hisses by forcing air out of the breathing holes along its body. Males hiss to warn rivals and to court females. It cannot fly and lives on the forest floor, eating rotting fruit and leaves.

name: Giraffe Weevil
entry: The male's neck is two to three times longer than the female's, and males use them to fight over mates. Females roll leaves into tubes to protect a single egg inside.

name: Comet Moth
entry: It is one of the largest silk moths in the world, with tails up to six inches long. The adult has no mouth and lives only four or five days.

name: Flatid Leaf Bug
entry: Adults gather on stems and line up so the whole group looks like a spike of pink flowers. The fluffy white nymphs coat themselves in threads of wax.

name: African Bombardier Beetle
entry: When attacked, it mixes chemicals in a chamber inside its body, causing a tiny explosion. It blasts out a spray at about 212°F and can aim it in almost any direction.

name: Saharan Silver Ant
entry: Triangular hairs make it shine like silver and reflect the sun's heat. It forages at midday, when the sand is too hot for its predators, running nearly three feet per second.

name: Deathstalker
entry: Its venom is among the most dangerous of any scorpion. Yet one compound in it, chlorotoxin, sticks to brain tumor cells, and scientists use it to make tumors glow for surgeons.

name: Darwin's Bark Spider
entry: Its silk is the toughest known biological material, about ten times tougher than Kevlar. It builds the largest orb webs on Earth, strung across rivers on bridge lines up to 80 feet long.

name: Orange Baboon Spider
entry: This bright orange tarantula is famous for its bad temper and rears up at the slightest disturbance. It lines its burrow with far more silk than most tarantulas.

name: Camel Spider
range: Deserts of North Africa & the Middle East
entry: It is neither a spider nor a scorpion. Its huge jaws can make up a third of its body length and chew through insects, lizards and even small birds. Stories say it chases people, but it is really following their shade.

name: Namib Wheel Spider
entry: When a wasp attacks, it tucks in its legs and cartwheels down the dune at over 40 turns per second. It lives in a silk-lined burrow dug into the sand.

name: Giant African Millipede
entry: It is one of the largest millipedes in the world, over a foot long with about 256 legs. When threatened, it curls into a spiral and oozes an irritating liquid.

name: Coconut Crab
range: Aldabra, the Seychelles & Indian Ocean islands
entry: It is the largest land invertebrate in the world. Its claws pinch with about the force of a lion's bite, enough to crack coconuts. It climbs trees and can live 60 years.

name: Peacock Mantis Shrimp
range: Indian Ocean, including the East African coast
entry: Its club-like arms strike so fast that the water around them boils into bubbles that burst with a flash of light. It smashes snail shells and can crack aquarium glass. Its eyes have up to 16 kinds of color receptors.

name: Horned Ghost Crab
range: Indian Ocean beaches, including East Africa
entry: Pale as the sand, it seems to vanish as it races across the beach at night. Long horns grow from the tips of its eyestalks. It is one of the fastest-running crabs.

name: Giant African Land Snail
range: Native to East Africa; invasive worldwide
entry: Its shell can grow nearly eight inches long. It eats hundreds of kinds of plants and can lay about 1,200 eggs a year, which makes it one of the world's worst invasive species.

name: Geography Cone
entry: It fires a venom-filled harpoon to catch fish. Its venom contains a form of insulin that sends nearby fish into shock. It is the most dangerous cone snail to humans.

name: Common Cuttlefish
range: Eastern Atlantic, including West & North Africa
entry: It changes its color, pattern and skin texture in a split second, even though it is colorblind. It has three hearts and blue-green blood.

name: Guinea Worm
range: A few places in Chad, Ethiopia & nearby countries
entry: People once caught it by drinking dirty water, and the worm later pushed out through a painful blister. A global campaign cut cases from millions a year to only a handful. It may become the first animal parasite wiped out by humans.

name: Coelacanth
range: Deep water off South Africa, Mozambique & the Comoros
entry: Scientists thought it had died out with the dinosaurs until one was caught off South Africa in 1938. Its fleshy, limb-like fins move in an alternating pattern, like the legs of a walking animal. It can live about 100 years.

name: Marbled Lungfish
range: Lakes & swamps of East & Central Africa
entry: When its swamp dries out, it burrows into the mud and wraps itself in a slime cocoon, breathing air through a small hole. It can survive this way for years. Its genome is one of the largest of any animal.

name: Electric Catfish
range: The Nile & rivers of tropical Africa
entry: It can release shocks of up to 350 volts to stun prey and defend itself. Ancient Egyptians painted it on tomb walls, and ancient doctors used its shocks to treat pain.

name: Elephantnose Fish
entry: It senses its surroundings with weak electric pulses and probes the mud for worms with its long chin. For its body size, its brain uses more oxygen than a human brain.

name: Tigerfish
range: Rivers & lakes of southern & central Africa
entry: It has rows of sharp, interlocking teeth. At a lake in South Africa it was filmed leaping out of the water to catch swallows in midair, the first freshwater fish known to do this.

name: Turquoise Killifish
entry: Its pools dry up after the rainy season, so it hatches, grows up and breeds within a few weeks. In the lab it lives only a few months, one of the shortest lifespans of any vertebrate. Its eggs wait out the dry season in the mud.

name: Great White Shark
range: Temperate seas, including South Africa's coast
entry: Off South Africa it hunts seals by charging up from below, sometimes launching its whole body out of the water. In recent years, orcas have driven great whites out of some South African bays by hunting them.

name: Devil Firefish
entry: Its long fin spines carry a painful venom. It spreads its wide fins to herd small fish into a corner before swallowing them. It has spread into the Mediterranean Sea through the Suez Canal.

name: Reef Stonefish
entry: It is the most venomous fish in the world. It looks exactly like an algae-covered rock, and the 13 spines on its back inject venom into anything that steps on it.

name: Atlantic Mudskipper
entry: It spends much of its time out of the water, hopping across the mud on its fins. It holds water in its gill chambers, breathes through its skin, and rolls in puddles to stay wet.

name: Knysna Seahorse
range: Three estuaries on South Africa's south coast
entry: It lives in only three estuaries in South Africa, which makes it one of the most endangered seahorses in the world. Like all seahorses, the male carries the eggs and gives birth.

name: African Bullfrog
entry: It can wait out the dry season underground for years inside a cocoon of shed skin. Males guard their tadpoles fiercely and may dig channels to lead them from a drying puddle to deeper water.

name: Goliath Frog
entry: It is the largest frog in the world, weighing up to seven pounds. Adults move rocks weighing more than half their own weight to build walled nest pools along riverbanks.

name: Hairy Frog
entry: When grabbed, it breaks the bones in its own toes to push sharp claws out through its skin. In breeding season, males grow hair-like strands of skin that help them take in oxygen.

name: Tomato Frog
entry: When threatened, it puffs up its bright red body. If a predator grabs it anyway, it oozes a thick, gluey slime that can gum the attacker's mouth and eyes shut.

name: Golden Mantella
entry: Its bright orange skin warns predators that it is toxic. It gets its poison from the ants and mites it eats, just like the unrelated poison frogs of Central and South America.

name: Taita Caecilian
entry: It looks like a worm but is a legless amphibian. The mother grows a thick, fatty outer layer of skin, and her babies peel it off and eat it with special teeth. She regrows it every few days.

name: Nile Crocodile
entry: It lies in wait at river crossings for zebras and wildebeest. Mothers guard their nests and gently carry newly hatched babies to the water in their mouths.

name: Panther Chameleon
entry: Its eyes swivel on their own, so it can look forward and backward at once. Males turn brilliant reds, blues and greens by rearranging tiny crystals in their skin. Its tongue can shoot out farther than its body is long.

name: Nosy Hara Leaf Chameleon
entry: It is one of the smallest reptiles on Earth, small enough to stand on the head of a match. By day it hides in leaf litter, and at night it climbs onto low twigs to sleep.

name: Satanic Leaf-tailed Gecko
entry: Its body and tail look exactly like a dead, curled leaf, complete with nicks and notches. If it is discovered, it opens its bright red mouth wide to startle the predator.

name: Namib Web-footed Gecko
entry: Its webbed feet work like snowshoes on sand and help it dig. It drinks by licking fog droplets off its own big eyes.

name: Shovel-snouted Lizard
entry: The sand it lives on can get hotter than 150°F. To keep from burning, it does a dance, lifting two feet at a time and switching. It dives headfirst into the sand to escape danger.

name: Armadillo Girdled Lizard
entry: When threatened, it bites its own tail and rolls into a spiky ball that protects its soft belly. Unlike most lizards, it lives in family groups.

name: Black Mamba
entry: It is one of the fastest snakes in the world. It is named for the inky black inside of its mouth, which it gapes as a warning. Without antivenom, its bite can kill within hours.

name: Gaboon Viper
entry: It has the longest fangs of any snake, up to two inches, and makes more venom than any other snake. Its patterned body vanishes among fallen leaves while it waits motionless for prey.

name: Mozambique Spitting Cobra
entry: It sprays venom from its fangs at an attacker's eyes from about eight feet away, tracking the target's head as it aims. Its bite is dangerous too.

name: African Rock Python
entry: It is Africa's largest snake and can swallow antelopes and even crocodiles whole. Unlike most snakes, the mother coils around her eggs and guards them until they hatch.

name: Pancake Tortoise
entry: Its shell is flat and bendy instead of hard and domed. When threatened, it runs into a rock crack and puffs up, wedging itself in so tightly it cannot be pulled out.

name: Aldabra Giant Tortoise
entry: It is one of the largest tortoises in the world and can live over 150 years. About 100,000 live on Aldabra, where their grazing has created a lawn of tiny plants called tortoise turf.

name: Shoebill
entry: It stands still for hours like a statue, then lunges to grab lungfish and catfish with its huge, shoe-shaped bill. Parents cool their chicks by pouring billfuls of water over them.

name: Secretarybird
entry: It hunts on foot, stomping on snakes and lizards. Each kick lasts only a few hundredths of a second and strikes with about five times its body weight.

name: Marabou Stork
entry: Its bald head and dark cloak of wings earned it the nickname undertaker bird. It feeds on carrion and garbage alongside vultures. Its wingspan can reach ten feet, among the largest of any land bird.

name: Common Ostrich
entry: It is the largest living bird and lays the biggest eggs of any bird. It cannot fly but can run over 40 miles per hour, and its kick can kill a lion.

name: Lesser Flamingo
range: Soda lakes of East & southern Africa
entry: Millions gather on salty lakes in East Africa to feed on spirulina. Most breed at Lake Natron, whose caustic water keeps predators away from their mud nests.

name: Grey Crowned Crane
range: Wetlands & grasslands of East & southern Africa
entry: It wears a crown of stiff golden feathers. Pairs bow, jump and dance together, and it is one of the only cranes that roosts in trees. It is the national bird of Uganda.

name: Southern Ground Hornbill
entry: Its deep booming calls carry for miles, and some cultures say they predict rain, earning it the name thunder bird. Family groups hunt on foot for snakes, tortoises and hares.

name: Grey Parrot
entry: It is one of the smartest birds. A grey parrot named Alex learned over 100 words and could name colors, shapes and numbers. Wild populations have fallen sharply because of the pet trade.

name: Greater Honeyguide
entry: It leads people to wild bee nests with a chattering call, then eats the wax once the honey hunters open the hive. It lays its eggs in other birds' nests, and its chick kills the host's chicks with a hooked bill.

name: Sociable Weaver
entry: Hundreds of birds build one huge grass nest together, the largest of any bird. A nest can weigh a ton and last over a century, staying warm on cold desert nights and cool at midday.

name: Bearded Vulture
entry: Bones make up most of its diet. It drops large bones onto rocks from high above to crack them, and its stomach acid dissolves the pieces. It dyes its feathers orange by bathing in iron-rich mud.

name: Egyptian Vulture
entry: It throws stones at ostrich eggs to crack them open, making it one of the few birds that use tools. Ancient Egyptians used its image as a letter in hieroglyphs.

name: Southern Carmine Bee-eater
entry: It catches bees and wasps in midair, then beats and rubs them on a branch to remove the stinger. Thousands nest together in tunnels dug into riverbanks. It sometimes rides on kori bustards to catch the insects they flush.

name: African Penguin
entry: It is the only penguin that breeds in Africa, feeding in the cold Benguela Current. Its loud braying call earned it the nickname jackass penguin. Pink skin above its eyes helps it shed heat on hot days.

name: Red-billed Quelea
entry: It is thought to be the most numerous wild bird on Earth, with over a billion adults. Flocks can take hours to fly past and are heavy enough to break tree branches.

name: Hamerkop
entry: Its head is shaped like a hammer. A pair builds an enormous domed nest of sticks and mud up to five feet across, and other animals often move in. In some folklore it is a bad omen.

name: African Bush Elephant
entry: It is the largest land animal on Earth, and its trunk contains tens of thousands of muscles. Elephants talk with low rumbles that travel for miles through the ground, and they may sense them through their feet.

name: Hippopotamus
entry: It spends its days in water and comes out at night to graze. Its skin oozes a red, oily fluid that works like sunscreen and fights germs. It is one of the most dangerous large animals in Africa.

name: White Rhinoceros
entry: Its horns are made of keratin, the same material as fingernails. Southern white rhinos fell to fewer than 100 around 1900 but recovered to thousands. The northern subspecies is down to its last two females.

name: Giraffe
entry: It is the tallest animal on Earth. Its neck has just seven bones, the same as a human's, but each one can be nearly a foot long. Its dark tongue is about 18 inches long.

name: Okapi
entry: It looks like a mix of zebra and deer, but its closest relative is the giraffe. It is so shy that scientists outside Africa did not know it existed until 1901. Its tongue is long enough to clean its own ears.

name: Lion
entry: It is the only truly social cat, living in family groups called prides. The females do most of the hunting together. A lion's roar can be heard up to five miles away.

name: Cheetah
range: Open plains of East & southern Africa
entry: It is the fastest land animal, reaching about 60 to 70 miles per hour in short bursts. Its long tail works as a rudder in sharp turns. Unlike other big cats, it cannot roar, but it chirps and purrs.

name: Leopard
entry: It is incredibly strong for its size and hauls its kills high into trees, away from lions and hyenas. It lives almost everywhere in Africa, from deserts to rainforests.

name: African Wild Dog
entry: Each dog's patchy coat pattern is unique. Packs hunt together and succeed far more often than lions. Before setting off on a hunt, pack members seem to vote by sneezing.

name: Spotted Hyena
entry: It is a skilled hunter, not just a scavenger, and its jaws crush bones to get at the marrow. Females are larger than males and lead the clan. Its giggling calls signal excitement or stress.

name: Meerkat
entry: While the group digs for food, one meerkat stands guard and calls out warnings about hawks and jackals. Adults teach pups to eat scorpions by first bringing them dead ones, then ones with the stinger removed.

name: Naked Mole-rat
entry: It lives in colonies ruled by a single queen, like bees. It can live over 30 years, almost never gets cancer, and can survive 18 minutes with no oxygen.

name: Aardvark
entry: Its name means earth pig in Afrikaans. It can eat tens of thousands of termites in a night with its sticky, foot-long tongue. The burrows it digs become homes for many other animals.

name: Temminck's Pangolin
entry: It is covered in overlapping scales made of keratin and rolls into a tight ball when threatened. It walks mostly on its hind legs. Pangolins are among the most trafficked mammals in the world.

name: Honey Badger
entry: It is famous for its fearlessness and will face lions and venomous snakes. Its loose, thick skin lets it twist around and bite an attacker that has grabbed it. It raids beehives for larvae and honey.

name: Aye-aye
entry: It taps on tree bark with its long, thin middle finger and listens for grubs hiding inside. Then it gnaws a hole and hooks them out. Some local legends say it brings bad luck.

name: Ring-tailed Lemur
entry: Males rub their long striped tails with scent from wrist glands, then wave them at rivals in stink fights. Groups are led by females. It sunbathes in the morning with its arms spread wide.

name: Fossa
entry: It is the largest predator on Madagascar and hunts lemurs high in the trees. Its ankles rotate so it can climb down trunks headfirst. It looks like a cat but is related to mongooses.

name: Mountain Gorilla
entry: It is the largest primate. A silverback leads each family group and beats his chest to show strength, yet it eats mostly leaves and stems. Protection efforts have helped its numbers grow past 1,000.

name: Chimpanzee
entry: It is one of our closest living relatives. Chimps strip twigs to fish termites out of mounds and crack nuts with stone hammers. Different groups have their own tool traditions, passed down like culture.

name: Bonobo
range: South of the Congo River, DR Congo
entry: It lives only south of the Congo River. Bonobo groups are led by females and settle conflicts by bonding rather than fighting. It shares nearly 99% of its DNA with humans.

name: Gelada
entry: It is the only primate that eats mostly grass. It lives in herds of hundreds on cold, high plateaus. The bare red patch on its chest brightens to show health and status, earning it the name bleeding-heart monkey.

name: Ethiopian Wolf
entry: It is Africa's most endangered carnivore, with only a few hundred left. It lives above the tree line in the cold highlands and hunts mole-rats alone, even though it lives in packs.

name: Fennec Fox
entry: It is the smallest fox in the world, with the biggest ears for its size. Its ears shed body heat and can hear prey moving underground. Fur on the soles of its feet protects them from burning sand.

name: Rock Hyrax
entry: It looks like a big guinea pig, but its closest living relatives are elephants and manatees. Colonies bask on rocks to warm up. They use the same latrine spots for thousands of years, building up rock-hard piles.

name: Blue Wildebeest
range: The Serengeti & Maasai Mara, East Africa
entry: Over a million make a yearly loop between Tanzania and Kenya, following the rains to fresh grass. Calves can stand within minutes of birth and keep up with the herd within days.

name: Plains Zebra
entry: No two zebras have the same stripes. The stripes seem to confuse biting flies, which often fail to land. A zebra's kick is strong enough to injure a lion.

name: Hammer-headed Bat
entry: It is Africa's largest bat. Males have huge heads and swollen lips that amplify their loud, honking calls. They gather along rivers at night and honk to attract females.

name: Cape Buffalo
entry: Hunters nicknamed it the black death because it is so dangerous. A herd will rally to defend a member under attack, and buffalo have been seen chasing lions off their kills.

name: Serval
entry: It has the longest legs for its size of any cat. It listens for rodents in tall grass, then leaps up to nine feet into the air to pounce. It can even knock birds out of the sky.

name: Dugong
range: The Red Sea & East African coast
entry: It grazes on sea grass, pulling up whole plants and leaving feeding trails across the sea floor. Its tail is fluked like a dolphin's. Sailors may once have mistaken dugongs for mermaids.

name: Grant's Golden Mole
entry: It is blind and has no visible ears, but it swims through loose sand and senses the faint vibrations of termites. Its fur shimmers with a greenish-bronze sheen.

name: Lowland Streaked Tenrec
entry: It rubs together special quills on its back to make a chirping sound, much like an insect. It is the only mammal known to communicate this way. Its striped quills also detach to defend it.

name: Mountain Ash
entry: It is the tallest flowering plant on Earth, with one tree in Tasmania over 330 feet tall. Its oily leaves help fires burn hot, and only a fierce fire opens its seed capsules so new trees can grow in the ash.

name: Rainbow Eucalyptus
entry: Its bark peels off in strips at different times, revealing fresh green bark that ages through blue, purple, orange and red. The trunk looks like it has been painted in stripes of color.

name: Wollemi Pine
range: One hidden canyon in Wollemi National Park, Australia
entry: Scientists knew it only from fossils up to 90 million years old until a park ranger found a living grove in 1994. Fewer than 100 wild trees exist, and their location is kept secret to protect them.

name: Grass Tree
entry: It grows only about an inch a year and can live for hundreds of years. After a bushfire, it shoots up a tall flower spike covered in thousands of tiny flowers. Its resin was used as glue by Aboriginal Australians.

name: Banksia
entry: Its flower spikes turn into woody cones that stay sealed for years. The heat of a bushfire opens them to release seeds. Honeyeaters and small mammals drink nectar from its brush-like flowers.

name: Gympie-gympie
entry: It has one of the most painful stings of any plant. Tiny silica hairs inject a toxin that can cause burning pain for weeks, flaring up again when the skin is touched or gets cold. Some pademelons eat its leaves without harm.

name: Kauri
entry: The largest living kauri, called Tāne Mahuta or Lord of the Forest, has a trunk over 50 feet around. Kauri can live over 2,000 years. Their resin, called kauri gum, was once dug up and sold to make varnish.

name: Silver Fern
entry: The undersides of its fronds are bright silver. Māori hunters and warriors laid them silver-side up to mark trails at night, because they reflect moonlight. It is a national symbol of New Zealand.

name: Albany Pitcher Plant
entry: Its tiny pitchers have toothed lids and pale windows that confuse trapped insects. It grows only in one corner of Australia and is not closely related to any other pitcher plant.

name: Triggerplant
entry: When an insect lands on its flower, a spring-loaded column snaps over in a fraction of a second and slaps pollen onto the insect's back. The trigger then slowly resets for the next visitor.

name: Kangaroo Paw
entry: Its fuzzy red-and-green flowers are shaped like a kangaroo's paw. Birds that perch on the stems to drink nectar get pollen brushed onto their heads. It is the floral emblem of Western Australia.

name: Haleakalā Silversword
range: Crater of Haleakalā volcano, Maui, Hawaii
entry: It grows only on the cinder slopes of one volcano. Silvery hairs on its leaves reflect the harsh mountain sun. After many decades, it sends up a single tall spike of hundreds of flowers, then dies.

name: Arctic Poppy
entry: Its cup-shaped yellow flower follows the sun around the sky during the endless Arctic summer day. The cup focuses heat onto its center, and insects bask inside it to warm up.

name: Arctic Willow
range: Arctic tundra of North America & Greenland
entry: It is a true tree, but it grows only a few inches tall and creeps along the ground out of the wind. It can live for hundreds of years. Its fuzzy catkins were used by the Inuit as lamp wicks.

name: Antarctic Hair Grass
entry: It is one of only two flowering plants that grow in Antarctica. It survives freezing temperatures and harsh sunlight, and it has spread quickly as the region has warmed.

name: Ghost Fungus
entry: Clusters of this pale, fan-shaped mushroom glow an eerie green in the dark forest. It grows on dead and dying trees. It is poisonous and causes vomiting if eaten.

name: Devil's Fingers
entry: It hatches from a jelly-filled egg in the soil and unfurls four to seven red arms like an octopus. The arms are coated with smelly slime that attracts flies, which carry away its spores.

name: Antarctic Lichen
entry: It clings to bare rock in one of the coldest, driest places on Earth and may grow less than a millimeter a century. It has survived being exposed to the vacuum of space in experiments.

name: Stromatolite Microbes
entry: These rocky mounds are built layer by layer by mats of cyanobacteria trapping sand. Similar structures are among the oldest evidence of life, over 3.5 billion years old. Their ancestors filled Earth's air with oxygen.

name: Arctic Woolly Bear
entry: It spends up to seven years as a caterpillar, freezing solid each winter and thawing out in spring. It feeds only for a few weeks each summer, slowly growing until it spins a cocoon and becomes a hairy moth that lives only a few days.

name: Arctic Bumblebee
range: Arctic tundra of North America, Greenland & Scandinavia
entry: It lives farther north than almost any other bee. It warms its flight muscles by shivering them without moving its wings and keeps a thick coat of hair. Queens rush through their whole nesting season in the short Arctic summer.

name: Antarctic Midge
entry: It is the only insect that lives year-round in Antarctica, and the continent's largest purely land animal at a quarter inch long. It has no wings, which keeps it from being blown away. Its larvae survive being frozen.

name: Snow Flea
range: Snowy forests of the Northern Hemisphere
entry: It is not a flea but a springtail, a tiny six-legged relative of insects. On warm winter days, millions come up and speckle the snow. It flings itself through the air with a spring-like tail folded under its body.

name: Lord Howe Island Stick Insect
range: Ball's Pyramid & Lord Howe Island, Australia
entry: It was thought extinct after rats reached its island in 1918. In 2001, climbers found about two dozen living under a single bush on Ball's Pyramid, a sea stack miles offshore. Zoos have since bred thousands.

name: Giant Wētā
entry: It is one of the heaviest insects in the world, and one female weighed more than a mouse. Its Māori name wētāpunga means god of ugly things. It filled the role mice play elsewhere before rats arrived in New Zealand.

name: Bogong Moth
entry: Each spring, billions fly up to 600 miles to cool caves in the Australian Alps to rest through summer. Experiments show they steer by the stars and Earth's magnetic field. Aboriginal people once gathered and roasted them in feasts.

name: Bull Ant
entry: It is one of the largest ants in the world, with long jaws and excellent eyesight. It hunts alone and delivers a very painful sting. It is known to chase intruders who come near its nest.

name: Queen Alexandra's Birdwing
range: Rainforests of Oro Province, Papua New Guinea
entry: It is the largest butterfly in the world, with females spanning up to 11 inches. The first specimen was shot down with a small shotgun. Its caterpillars eat toxic vines, making the adults poisonous to birds.

name: New Zealand Glowworm
range: Caves & damp gullies of New Zealand
entry: It is the larva of a fungus gnat. It hangs dozens of sticky silk threads from cave ceilings and glows blue to lure flying insects into them. Thousands together make caves look like a starry night sky.

name: Ulysses Butterfly
entry: Its wings flash electric blue in flight, but the undersides are dull brown, so it seems to vanish when it lands. Males are attracted to anything bright blue and will even chase blue objects.

name: Magnetic Termite
entry: Its mounds are thin wedges, up to 13 feet tall, all lined up north to south. This keeps the broad sides facing the gentle morning and evening sun while the narrow edge faces the fierce midday heat.

name: Spiny Leaf Insect
entry: It looks like a dry, spiky leaf and curls its abdomen over its back like a scorpion when disturbed. Females can lay eggs without males. Ants carry the eggs into their nests, where the babies hatch safely.

name: Giant Jewel Beetle
entry: Males were found trying to mate with discarded brown beer bottles, which had bumps and a shine like a large female. The discovery won an Ig Nobel Prize, and bottle makers changed their design.

name: Leichhardt's Grasshopper
entry: It is bright orange and blue and feeds on toxic shrubs. Aboriginal people call it the children of Namarrkon, the Lightning Man, because it appears in larger numbers just before the monsoon storms.

name: Sydney Funnel-web Spider
entry: Its venom is especially dangerous to humans and other primates, though harmless to many other animals. Males wander at night looking for mates and sometimes fall into swimming pools. An antivenom made in 1981 has prevented deaths since.

name: Peacock Spider
entry: The male is smaller than a grain of rice. To court a female, he raises a colorful fan on his abdomen and dances, waving his legs. If she is not impressed, she may eat him.

name: Redback Spider
entry: The female is black with a red stripe on her back. She often hides in sheds, mailboxes and under outdoor furniture. The male flips his body into her fangs while mating and is often eaten.

name: Antarctic Krill
entry: It forms swarms so dense they can be seen from space, and its total weight may be among the largest of any wild animal. Whales, seals, penguins and fish all depend on it. It can shrink when food runs short.

name: Christmas Island Red Crab
entry: Each year, tens of millions march from the forest to the sea to spawn, covering roads, and islanders build bridges and tunnels for them. It spends the rest of the year eating leaf litter on the forest floor.

name: Colossal Squid
entry: It is the heaviest invertebrate known. Its eyes are the largest in the animal kingdom, about the size of a soccer ball. Its arms carry swiveling hooks. It was first filmed alive in its deep-sea home in 2025.

name: Blue Dragon
range: Warm oceans; often washes up in eastern Australia
entry: This small blue sea slug floats upside down on the ocean surface. It eats Portuguese man o' war and stores their stinging cells in its own fingertips, so its sting can be even more powerful.

name: Giant Australian Cuttlefish
entry: It is the largest cuttlefish in the world. Each winter, thousands gather near Whyalla to breed. Small males sneak past big rivals by disguising themselves as females, changing their color and hiding their arms.

name: Kauri Snail
range: Kauri forests of northern New Zealand
entry: This giant land snail is a meat eater. It hunts earthworms at night and slurps them up like spaghetti. Its shell can be three inches across.

name: Giant Clam
range: Reefs of the western Pacific & Great Barrier Reef
entry: It is the largest clam in the world, over four feet long and 500 pounds. Algae living in its colorful mantle make food from sunlight. Despite myths, it cannot trap divers because it closes very slowly.

name: Sea Pig
range: Deep sea floors, including around Antarctica
entry: This deep-sea cucumber walks on inflated tube feet that work like legs. Herds of sea pigs roam the muddy abyss, facing into the current to smell food. Tiny crabs sometimes ride underneath them.

name: Australian Box Jellyfish
entry: It is one of the most venomous animals in the world. It has 24 eyes, some with lenses, and can swim fast enough to hunt fish. Its see-through body makes it nearly invisible in the water.

name: Giant Gippsland Earthworm
entry: It can grow over three feet long and lives in deep, wet burrows. It moves so quickly through its slimy tunnels that people can hear gurgling sounds underground. It can live for decades.

name: Leafy Seadragon
entry: Leafy flaps all over its body make it look like floating seaweed. It moves by rippling tiny, see-through fins on its neck and back. The male carries the eggs stuck to the underside of his tail.

name: Australian Lungfish
entry: It has barely changed in over 100 million years. It uses a single lung to breathe air when water is low. A lungfish named Granddad lived at an aquarium in Chicago for over 80 years.

name: Blobfish
range: Deep waters off southeastern Australia & New Zealand
entry: In the deep sea, it looks like a normal fish. Its jelly-like body only turns into a droopy blob when pulled to the surface. It was voted the world's ugliest animal in 2013.

name: Orange Clownfish
range: Great Barrier Reef, New Guinea & the western Pacific
entry: It lives safely among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, protected by a special mucus. All clownfish hatch male. When the female of a group dies, the largest male turns into a female.

name: Blackfin Icefish
entry: It is one of the only vertebrates with no red blood cells, so its blood is clear. It survives because icy Antarctic water holds lots of oxygen, and it has a huge heart to pump its thin blood.

name: Southern Corroboree Frog
entry: It is bright yellow with black stripes and lives in alpine bogs. Unlike most poison frogs, it makes its own toxin instead of getting it from its food. Fewer than 100 remain in the wild due to a skin fungus.

name: Gastric-brooding Frog
entry: The mother swallowed her fertilized eggs and raised the tadpoles in her stomach, which stopped making acid. After about six weeks, she gave birth to baby frogs through her mouth. It went extinct in the 1980s.

name: Water-holding Frog
entry: After rain, it fills its body and bladder with water, then burrows into the ground and seals itself in a cocoon of shed skin. It can wait underground for years until the next rain comes.

name: Turtle Frog
entry: It looks like a small turtle without a shell. Unlike most burrowing frogs, it digs headfirst with its strong front legs. Its eggs hatch as fully formed froglets underground, with no tadpole stage.

name: White's Tree Frog
entry: This plump green frog often lives around houses, in toilets, gutters and water tanks. Its skin makes compounds that fight bacteria and viruses, which scientists study for medicines. It can live over 20 years.

name: Archey's Frog
entry: It belongs to one of the most ancient frog families alive, little changed in 200 million years. It has no tadpole stage. The father guards the eggs, then carries the tiny froglets on his back.

name: Thorny Devil
entry: It is covered in cone-shaped spikes. Tiny grooves between its scales soak up water from dew or wet sand and carry it to its mouth. It eats thousands of ants a day and has a fake head on its neck.

name: Frilled Lizard
entry: When threatened, it opens a huge frill of skin around its neck, gapes its yellow mouth and hisses. If that fails, it runs away on its hind legs like a tiny dinosaur.

name: Tuatara
entry: It looks like a lizard but is the last survivor of a group of reptiles that lived with the dinosaurs. Young tuatara have a third eye on top of their heads. It can live over 100 years and keeps growing until age 35.

name: Inland Taipan
entry: It has the most toxic venom of any land snake, tested on mice. Yet it is shy and rarely bites people, living in remote deserts. Its skin darkens in winter to soak up more heat.

name: Shingleback Lizard
entry: Its thick, scaly body looks like a pinecone, and its stubby tail looks like a second head. Pairs reunite every spring for decades, and partners stay close together, even walking one behind the other.

name: Blue-tongued Skink
entry: When threatened, it puffs up, hisses and sticks out its bright blue tongue to startle predators. The tongue also reflects ultraviolet light. Mothers give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

name: Mary River Turtle
entry: It can stay underwater for up to three days by breathing through special organs in its rear end. Algae often grows on its head like a green mohawk. It was once sold as a pet before scientists knew what it was.

name: Green Tree Python
range: Rainforests of New Guinea & northern Australia
entry: Babies are born bright yellow or red and turn green as they grow up. It rests coiled over a branch in a neat saddle shape. It wiggles the tip of its tail like a worm to lure prey.

name: Perentie
entry: It is Australia's largest lizard, reaching eight feet long. It stands up on its hind legs to look around. It hunts rabbits, reptiles and birds, and uses its tail as a whip in fights.

name: Fiji Crested Iguana
entry: It is bright green with white bands and can turn black in seconds when threatened. Its ancestors may have rafted all the way from the Americas. Its eggs take up to nine months to hatch, one of the longest of any lizard.

name: Emperor Penguin Chick
entry: It hatches in the dark Antarctic winter and spends its first weeks on its parent's feet, tucked under a warm flap of skin. Chicks gather in groups called crèches to stay warm while the parents fish.

name: Emperor Penguin
entry: It is the largest penguin and the only animal that breeds on open Antarctic ice in winter. The father balances the egg on his feet for about two months without eating, huddling with thousands of others in temperatures below -40°F.

name: Adélie Penguin
entry: It builds its nest from pebbles, and neighbors often steal stones from each other. Males may offer pebbles to females. It walks great distances across the ice to reach the sea.

name: Little Penguin
entry: It is the smallest penguin in the world, only about a foot tall, with slate-blue feathers. At dusk, groups waddle up the beach together to their burrows in a nightly parade that tourists come to watch.

name: Snow Petrel
entry: It is pure white and nests on cliffs deep inside Antarctica. To defend itself, it spits a smelly stomach oil at intruders. Over thousands of years, the oil builds up into waxy deposits near nests that scientists use to study past climate.

name: Wandering Albatross
entry: It has the largest wingspan of any living bird, up to 11 feet. It can glide for hours without flapping and may fly around the whole Southern Ocean in a few weeks. Pairs mate for life and dance when they reunite.

name: Arctic Tern
range: Breeds in the Arctic; winters off Antarctica
entry: It makes the longest migration of any animal, flying from the Arctic to Antarctica and back each year. Over a lifetime, one tern may fly distances equal to three trips to the Moon and back. It sees more daylight than any other animal.

name: Rock Ptarmigan
entry: It turns pure white in winter and mottled brown in summer to match its surroundings. Feathers cover its feet like snowshoes. In winter it burrows into snowbanks to sleep.

name: Ivory Gull
entry: This all-white gull spends its whole life near the Arctic sea ice. It follows polar bears to feed on the leftovers of their seal kills. Its numbers have dropped sharply as the sea ice shrinks.

name: Gyrfalcon
entry: It is the largest falcon in the world and comes in white, gray and dark forms. It hunts ptarmigan across the tundra in fast, low chases. Medieval kings prized white gyrfalcons for hunting.

name: Southern Brown Kiwi
entry: It is the only bird with nostrils at the tip of its bill, which it uses to sniff out worms underground. The female lays one of the largest eggs for her size of any bird, about a fifth of her body weight.

name: Kākāpō
entry: It is the world's only flightless parrot and the heaviest parrot. It smells musty-sweet like honey. Down to about 50 birds in 1995, it has recovered to over 200, and every bird has a name.

name: Kea
entry: It is the only alpine parrot in the world and lives in snowy mountains. It is curious and clever, known for tearing apart car wipers and backpacks. Its laugh-like call can make other kea playful.

name: Emu
entry: It is the second-largest bird in the world and can run over 30 miles per hour. The father sits on the dark green eggs for about eight weeks without eating. In 1932, Australian soldiers lost the so-called Emu War.

name: Southern Cassowary
range: Rainforests of northeastern Australia & New Guinea
entry: It has a five-inch dagger-like claw on each foot and a bony helmet on its head. It is one of the most dangerous birds but mostly eats fruit, spreading the seeds of many rainforest trees.

name: Superb Lyrebird
entry: It is one of the best mimics in the animal world. Males copy the calls of dozens of other birds, and some have imitated camera shutters and chainsaws. It dances with its lacy tail fanned over its head.

name: Laughing Kookaburra
entry: Its loud laughing call rings out at dawn and dusk, earning it the name bushman's clock. It is a giant kingfisher that hunts snakes, lizards and insects, beating them against a branch before eating.

name: Superb Bird-of-paradise
entry: To court a female, the male raises a cape of ultra-black feathers into an oval and flashes a blue-green breast shield, making a shape like a smiling face. His black feathers absorb over 99% of light.

name: Satin Bowerbird
entry: The male builds an avenue of sticks called a bower and decorates it with blue objects like flowers, feathers and bottle caps. He even paints the walls with chewed-up berries. Females inspect several bowers before choosing a mate.

name: Hooded Pitohui
entry: It was the first bird known to be poisonous. Its skin and feathers contain a toxin like that of poison dart frogs, which it gets from the beetles it eats. Touching it can make your hands numb.

name: Malleefowl
entry: The male builds a huge mound of sand and rotting leaves that warms the eggs like a compost heap. He checks the temperature by sticking his beak into the mound and adds or removes sand to keep it just right.

name: Takahē
entry: This large, flightless, blue-green bird was declared extinct in 1898. In 1948, a doctor rediscovered a small population in a remote valley in the mountains. Careful protection has brought it back to about 500.

name: Palm Cockatoo
entry: The male breaks off a stick, shapes it, and drums it against a hollow tree to attract females. Each bird has its own drumming style. Its red cheeks flush brighter when it gets excited.

name: Nēnē
entry: It is the rarest goose in the world and Hawaii's state bird. Its feet have less webbing than other geese, helping it walk on rough lava fields. Only about 30 were left in 1952, but breeding programs saved it.

name: Great Frigatebird
entry: It chases other seabirds until they drop their fish, then snatches the food in midair. It can stay aloft for weeks, even taking short naps while flying. Males inflate a huge red throat pouch to attract females.

name: Australian Magpie
entry: During nesting season, some males swoop at people who walk too close. It remembers individual human faces for years, attacking some and ignoring friends. Its warbling song is one of the most complex of any bird.

name: Kererū
entry: This large pigeon is one of the only birds left that can swallow New Zealand's biggest forest fruits and spread their seeds. It sometimes eats fermented fruit, gets tipsy, and falls out of trees.

name: Black Swan
entry: Europeans believed all swans were white until explorers saw black swans in Australia in 1697, so a black swan came to mean something unexpected. Pairs raise their cygnets together and often stay partners for life.

name: Rainbow Lorikeet
entry: Its feathers are a riot of blue, green, orange and yellow. It has a brush-tipped tongue for lapping up nectar and pollen. Large noisy flocks gather in city trees at dusk.

name: Tawny Frogmouth
entry: It looks like an owl but is related to nightjars. By day, it freezes on a branch with its eyes closed and bill pointed up, looking exactly like a dead stump. At night, it catches insects and mice with its wide mouth.

name: Platypus
entry: It is a mammal that lays eggs, has a bill like a duck and senses the electric fields of prey. Males have venomous spurs on their back legs. Under ultraviolet light, its fur glows blue-green.

name: Short-beaked Echidna
entry: It is one of only a few mammals that lay eggs. The female lays a single leathery egg into a pouch on her belly. The baby, called a puggle, grows in the pouch until its spines start to grow.

name: Koala
entry: It eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves, which are tough and toxic to most animals. The leaves give little energy, so it sleeps up to 20 hours a day. It is a marsupial, not a bear.

name: Red Kangaroo Joey
entry: It is born the size of a jellybean and crawls into its mother's pouch, where it grows for about eight months. Even after leaving, it dives back into the pouch headfirst when scared.

name: Red Kangaroo
entry: It is the largest marsupial and can bound 25 feet in a single hop. Males box each other, balancing on their tails to deliver powerful kicks. A mother can pause the growth of an embryo until conditions improve.

name: Tasmanian Devil
entry: It has one of the strongest bites for its size of any mammal and eats bones, fur and all. It screeches and growls when feeding. A contagious face cancer has killed most wild devils since the 1990s.

name: Quokka
entry: This small wallaby seems to smile, making it famous for selfies with tourists. Dutch explorers thought it was a giant rat and named Rottnest Island, meaning rat's nest, after it.

name: Common Wombat
entry: It is the only animal that makes cube-shaped droppings, which it stacks on rocks to mark territory. Its rump is made of tough cartilage, which it uses to block its burrow. Its pouch faces backward so dirt stays out while it digs.

name: Sugar Glider
entry: It glides between trees on flaps of skin stretched from its wrists to its ankles, traveling over 150 feet. It loves sweet sap and nectar, which gave it its name. Its fur glows pink under ultraviolet light.

name: Numbat
entry: This striped marsupial eats up to 20,000 termites a day, licking them up with a long, sticky tongue. Unlike most marsupials, it is active during the day. It is the animal emblem of Western Australia.

name: Thylacine
entry: This striped marsupial predator looked like a dog but carried its young in a pouch. The last known thylacine died in a zoo in 1936. People still report sightings, but none have ever been confirmed.

name: Goodfellow's Tree-kangaroo
entry: This kangaroo lives in treetops and can leap 30 feet down to the ground without getting hurt. Its long tail helps it balance on branches. Unlike ground kangaroos, it can walk and move its legs one at a time.

name: Dingo
entry: It arrived in Australia with seafaring people at least 3,500 years ago and became Australia's top land predator. It rarely barks, howling instead. Its flexible joints let it turn its paws to climb and grip.

name: Greater Bilby
entry: It has long rabbit-like ears and digs spiral burrows up to six feet deep. Australians sell chocolate bilbies at Easter instead of bunnies to raise money for protecting it from foxes and feral cats.

name: Grey-headed Flying Fox
entry: It is Australia's largest bat, with a wingspan over three feet. It finds food by sight and smell, not echolocation. Flying up to 30 miles a night, it pollinates eucalyptus trees and spreads rainforest seeds.

name: Southern Marsupial Mole
entry: It is blind, has no external ears, and swims through desert sand, which collapses behind it. Its pouch faces backward to keep sand out. It is so rarely seen that little is known about its life.

name: Honey Possum
entry: It is one of the only mammals that feeds only on nectar and pollen. It has a brush-tipped tongue and a grasping tail. Males have the longest sperm of any mammal, longer than those of a whale.

name: Hector's Dolphin
entry: It is one of the smallest dolphins in the world, with a round fin shaped like Mickey Mouse's ear. It lives only around New Zealand, and its rarest form, Māui dolphin, has fewer than 60 left.

name: Common Spotted Cuscus
entry: This slow, round-faced marsupial has big red-rimmed eyes and a grasping tail. It spends the day curled in the treetops and eats leaves and fruit at night. Only males have spots.

name: Greater Glider
entry: It glides up to 300 feet between trees using skin flaps stretched from elbow to ankle. It eats only eucalyptus leaves. Scientists found in 2020 that it is actually three separate species.

name: Spinifex Hopping Mouse
entry: It hops on its long back legs like a tiny kangaroo. Its kidneys concentrate its urine more than any other mammal's, so it can survive without ever drinking water.

name: Arctic Fox
entry: Its thick coat turns white in winter and brown in summer. It can survive temperatures of -58°F and follows polar bears to eat their leftovers. One arctic fox walked over 2,700 miles from Norway to Canada in 76 days.

name: Muskox
entry: Its underwool, qiviut, is warmer than sheep's wool and softer than cashmere. When wolves attack, the herd forms a circle with horns facing out and the calves in the middle. It survived the Ice Age alongside mammoths.

name: Bowhead Whale
entry: It may be the longest-lived mammal, with some over 200 years old. Old harpoon tips from the 1800s have been found in living whales. It breaks through sea ice up to two feet thick with its massive head.

name: Beluga
entry: Its chirps, whistles and clicks earned it the nickname sea canary. Unlike most whales, it can turn its head. One beluga in captivity learned to imitate the rhythms of human speech.

name: Arctic Hare
entry: It can run over 35 miles per hour and sometimes hops on its hind legs like a kangaroo. Groups of hundreds huddle together for warmth. It digs through snow to reach willow twigs to eat.

name: Ringed Seal
entry: It keeps breathing holes open in thick sea ice by scraping with its claws. Mothers give birth in hidden lairs dug in the snow on top of the ice. It is the main food of polar bears.

name: Arctic Ground Squirrel
range: Arctic tundra of Alaska, Canada & Siberia
entry: During hibernation, its body temperature drops below freezing, to about 27°F, the coldest of any mammal, yet its blood does not freeze. Every few weeks it shivers to warm up briefly, then cools down again.

name: Leopard Seal
entry: It is the top predator of Antarctic waters after the orca, hunting penguins and other seals. Its back teeth lock together into a sieve, so it can also filter krill from the water.

name: Weddell Seal
entry: It lives farther south than any other mammal. It keeps breathing holes open by grinding the ice with its teeth. Under the ice, it sings eerie trills and whistles that can be heard through the ice above.

name: Crabeater Seal
entry: Despite its name, it eats almost no crabs. It strains krill from the water through its uniquely shaped, lobed teeth. It may be one of the most numerous large mammals on Earth.

name: Humpback Whale
range: All oceans; feeds in Antarctic waters
entry: Males sing long, complex songs that change over time and spread from one population to another. Groups work together to blow rings of bubbles that trap fish before they lunge up through the middle to eat.

name: Loggerhead Hatchling
range: Hatches on beaches in Florida, Oman & Australia; grows up at sea
entry: It digs out of its nest at night and races to the sea by moonlight. It then drifts for years among floating seaweed in the open ocean, a period scientists call the lost years. It reads Earth's magnetic field like a map.

name: Loggerhead Sea Turtle
entry: Its huge head holds jaws strong enough to crush conch shells and crabs. Females return to nest on the same beach where they hatched, sometimes crossing an entire ocean to get there.

name: Phyllosoma
range: Open ocean of the western Atlantic
entry: The spiny lobster starts life as a flat, see-through larva shaped like a leaf with long legs. It drifts in the open ocean for up to a year, sometimes riding on jellyfish, before settling on a reef.

name: Caribbean Spiny Lobster
entry: It has no big claws, but it screeches by rubbing its antennae to scare predators. Each autumn, lobsters march across the sea floor in single-file lines of up to 50, touching the one in front.

name: Moon Jelly Polyp
entry: The moon jelly begins as a tiny polyp stuck to a rock. It can clone itself for years. When the water warms, its body divides into a stack of discs, like a pile of plates.

name: Moon Jelly Ephyra
entry: Each disc of the polyp breaks free and swims away as an ephyra, a tiny eight-armed star. It pulses through the water catching plankton and slowly grows into a round jellyfish.

name: Moon Jelly
entry: It has four horseshoe-shaped rings in its bell, which are its reproductive organs. It has no brain, heart or blood. Huge blooms have clogged the cooling pipes of power plants and shut them down.

name: Krøyer's Deep Sea Anglerfish
entry: The tiny male bites onto the much larger female and fuses with her body, sharing her blood for the rest of his life. A female can be over 500,000 times heavier than her mate.

name: Black Seadevil
entry: It dangles a glowing lure lit by bacteria in front of its huge mouth full of needle teeth. Its stomach stretches so much that it can swallow prey bigger than itself. It was first filmed alive in 2014.

name: Sloane's Viperfish
entry: Its fangs are so long they cannot fit inside its mouth and curve up past its eyes. It uses a glowing spine on its back as a lure. At night, it rises hundreds of feet toward the surface to feed.

name: Gulper Eel
entry: Its enormous mouth unhinges like a pelican's pouch and is far bigger than the rest of its body. Its long whip of a tail ends in a pink glowing tip that may lure prey.

name: Common Fangtooth
entry: For its size, it has the largest teeth of any fish in the ocean. The two biggest fangs slide into sockets on either side of its brain when it closes its mouth. It lives as deep as 16,000 feet.

name: Giant Oarfish
entry: It is the longest bony fish in the world, reaching over 26 feet, with a red crest like a mane. It swims upright and may be behind many sea serpent legends. In Japan, it is said to warn of earthquakes.

name: Tripod Fish
entry: It stands on the sea floor on three long, stiff fin rays like a tripod, facing into the current. It holds its front fins up like antennae to feel for small animals drifting past.

name: Mariana Snailfish
entry: It lives deeper than almost any other fish, over 26,000 feet down, where pressure is over 800 times that at the surface. Its soft, see-through pink body and flexible bones help it survive.

name: Megamouth Shark
entry: It was unknown to science until one got tangled in a US Navy anchor off Hawaii in 1976. Only a few hundred have ever been seen. It swims with its huge mouth open, filtering krill and jellies.

name: Cookiecutter Shark
entry: It latches onto whales, dolphins and large fish with its lips, then spins to carve out a round plug of flesh. It has even bitten the rubber coverings of submarines. Its belly glows to hide it from below.

name: Opah
entry: It is the first fish known to be fully warm-blooded. Its flapping fin muscles make heat, and special blood vessels keep it inside, so it stays warm and quick in cold deep water. It is round like a dinner plate.

name: Basking Shark
entry: It is the second-largest fish in the world. It swims slowly near the surface with its huge mouth wide open, filtering about 2,000 tons of water an hour for tiny plankton.

name: Giant Oceanic Manta Ray
entry: It is the largest ray, with wings up to 23 feet across, and has one of the largest brains of any fish. In tests with mirrors, mantas behaved as if they might recognize themselves.

name: Brownsnout Spookfish
entry: It is the only vertebrate known to use mirrors instead of lenses to focus light in its eyes. Each eye is split in two, one part looking up and the other using a curved mirror to see flashes from below.

name: Tiger Shark
entry: It eats almost anything, including sea turtles, seabirds and even license plates and tires. Its serrated teeth can saw through turtle shells. Young sharks have dark stripes that fade with age.

name: Vampire Squid
entry: Its name means vampire squid from hell, but it eats only marine snow, the falling bits of dead matter. When threatened, it turns its webbed arms inside out like a cloak and releases glowing mucus instead of ink.

name: Dumbo Octopus
entry: It flaps two ear-like fins on its head to swim, like the flying elephant Dumbo. It lives deeper than any other octopus, down to about 23,000 feet, and swallows its prey whole.

name: Giant Squid
entry: It may have inspired legends of the kraken. It can grow over 40 feet long, and its eyes are as big as dinner plates. Scientists filmed one alive in its deep-sea home for the first time in 2012.

name: Glass Octopus
entry: It is almost completely see-through. Only its eyes, optic nerves and digestive gland are visible. Its eyes are rectangular and can rotate to cast a thinner shadow to predators below.

name: Bigfin Squid
entry: Its arms and tentacles bend out at sharp angles like elbows and trail below it for up to 25 feet. It has been filmed only a handful of times by deep-sea robots, and no adult has ever been caught.

name: Greater Argonaut
entry: The female octopus makes a thin, paper-like white shell with two special arms to hold her eggs. She traps air inside it to float. The male is tiny and never builds a shell.

name: Blanket Octopus
entry: The female can be up to 40,000 times heavier than the male. She unfurls a huge, colorful web like a blanket to look bigger. Young ones carry torn tentacles of Portuguese man o' war as weapons.

name: Portuguese Man O' War
entry: It is not a jellyfish but a colony of many small animals working as one. A gas-filled float acts as a sail, and its stinging tentacles can trail 100 feet below. It stings even after washing up dead.

name: Giant Siphonophore
entry: It is one of the longest animals on Earth, reaching over 130 feet. It is a chain of thousands of clones, each specialized to swim, sting, eat or reproduce. It glows blue when disturbed.

name: Pyrosome
entry: Its name means fire body. It is a hollow tube made of thousands of tiny clones that glow brightly when touched. Giant pyrosomes over 60 feet long have been seen, big enough for a diver to swim inside.

name: Atolla Jellyfish
entry: When attacked, it flashes a spinning ring of blue lights. This burglar alarm may attract bigger predators to eat whatever is attacking it. Its red body is invisible in the deep, where red light does not reach.

name: Giant Phantom Jelly
entry: Its bell can be three feet wide, and its four ribbon-like mouth arms trail over 30 feet. It has been seen only about 100 times in over a century, mostly by deep-sea robots.

name: Bone-eating Worm
range: Whale bones on deep sea floors
entry: It has no mouth or stomach. It grows root-like tissue into the bones of dead whales and uses acid to dissolve them, while bacteria inside it digest the fats. It looks like a tuft of red flowers.

name: Giant Tube Worm
range: Hydrothermal vents of the eastern Pacific
entry: It grows up to eight feet long near scalding volcanic vents. It has no mouth or gut. Its red plume, full of blood, soaks up chemicals from the water that bacteria inside it turn into food.

name: Pompeii Worm
range: Hydrothermal vents of the eastern Pacific
entry: It lives in tubes on the walls of hot volcanic chimneys and may be one of the most heat-tolerant complex animals on Earth. A fleece of bacteria on its back may act like a heat shield.

name: Scaly-foot Snail
range: Hydrothermal vents of the Indian Ocean
entry: It is the only animal known to build its armor from iron. Its shell and the scales on its foot are coated in iron sulfide. It gets food from bacteria living inside a giant gland in its throat.

name: Yeti Crab
range: Deep-sea vents & seeps of the South Pacific
entry: Its arms are covered in long, silky hairs. It grows bacteria on the hairs and waves its arms over the vents to feed them chemicals, then eats the bacteria. It is blind.

name: Giant Isopod
range: Deep sea floors of the Atlantic
entry: This relative of pill bugs grows over a foot long in the deep sea. It scavenges on dead whales and fish that sink. One in a Japanese aquarium went more than five years without eating.

name: Headless Chicken Monster
entry: This see-through, reddish sea cucumber looks like a plucked chicken ready for the oven. Unlike most sea cucumbers, it can swim, flapping webbed fins to lift off the sea floor.

name: Harp Sponge
