entry: This carnivorous sponge grows upright branches shaped like the strings of a harp. Tiny hooks on the branches snag small crustaceans, which the sponge then wraps in a thin film and digests.

name: Sea Sparkle
entry: This single-celled plankton glows blue whenever the water around it moves. During huge blooms, crashing waves and footprints on the beach light up in electric blue.

name: Deepstaria
entry: This jellyfish has no tentacles. Its huge, thin bell billows like a plastic bag and closes around prey. A delicate net of canals spreads across the bell like a spider web.

name: Telescope Octopus
entry: It is the only octopus with tube-shaped eyes that can rotate on stalks. Its see-through, jelly-like body floats in the open ocean. Its eyes let it look up at prey silhouetted against faint light.

name: Xenophyophore
range: Deep sea floors, including the deepest trenches
entry: Each one is a single cell that can grow as big as a fist, making it one of the largest single cells on Earth. It builds a crumbly shell out of sand and mud. Many tiny animals live inside its shell.

name: Olive Ridley Sea Turtle
range: Tropical oceans; nests in Mexico, Costa Rica & India
entry: It is known for the arribada, meaning arrival, when hundreds of thousands of females come ashore together over a few nights to lay eggs on the same beach.

name: Sea Sapphire
entry: Males of this tiny copepod flash brilliant blue, gold and violet as they swim. Layers of crystals in their backs reflect light, and by turning slightly, they can seem to vanish completely.

name: Sperm Whale
entry: It has the largest brain of any animal. It dives over a mile deep to hunt giant squid, and its clicks are the loudest sounds made by any animal. Family groups communicate in patterns of clicks called codas.

name: Cuvier's Beaked Whale
entry: It holds the record for the deepest and longest dives of any mammal, reaching nearly two miles down and staying under for almost four hours. It is rarely seen at the surface.

name: Fin Whale
entry: It is the second-largest animal on Earth and one of the fastest whales. Its right jaw is white and its left jaw is dark, which may help it herd fish. Its deep calls can travel hundreds of miles.

name: Gray Whale
entry: It makes one of the longest migrations of any mammal, up to 14,000 miles a year between Alaska and Mexico. It feeds by sucking mud from the sea floor. Its skin is covered in barnacles and whale lice.

name: Northern Elephant Seal
entry: It spends months at sea, diving almost nonstop. During deep dives, it sometimes falls asleep and drifts down in a slow spiral, getting just two hours of sleep a day. It was once hunted down to fewer than 100.

name: Green Sea Turtle
entry: It is named for the green color of its fat, which comes from a diet of seagrass and algae. It swims thousands of miles between feeding grounds and the beaches where it nests.

name: Hawksbill Sea Turtle
entry: It eats sponges full of glass-like spikes and toxins that most animals avoid. In 2015, divers filmed one glowing red and green, the first reptile seen to glow this way in the wild.

name: Sooty Tern
entry: Young sooty terns may stay in the air for three to ten years without landing, because their feathers are not waterproof. They sleep in short bursts while flying.

name: Wilson's Storm Petrel
entry: It flutters over the waves with its feet pattering on the water, as if walking on it. It may be one of the most numerous birds in the world, flying from Antarctica to the North Atlantic each year.

name: Northern Gannet
entry: It plunges into the sea from up to 100 feet high, hitting the water at about 60 miles per hour. Air sacs under its skin cushion the impact, and it has no external nostrils to keep water out.

name: Laysan Albatross
entry: A Laysan albatross named Wisdom is the oldest known wild bird, still laying eggs past the age of 70. She has flown millions of miles in her lifetime, roaming the North Pacific for months at a time.

name: Red-billed Tropicbird
entry: This white seabird has a bright red bill and two tail streamers longer than its body. It plunges into the sea for flying fish and squid. On land, it can barely walk and must shuffle on its belly.

name: Atlantic Puffin
entry: Its colorful bill fades each winter and brightens again for breeding season. It can carry over a dozen small fish at once, held crosswise in its bill by a spiny tongue. It spends winters far out at sea.

name: Sooty Shearwater
range: Oceans worldwide; nests in New Zealand & Chile
entry: It flies a giant figure-eight route across the Pacific each year, about 40,000 miles. It can also dive over 200 feet underwater, using its wings to swim after fish and squid.

name: Red Phalarope
range: Breeds in the Arctic; winters at sea
entry: It spins in tight circles on the water's surface, creating a small whirlpool that pulls plankton up to its bill. Females are more colorful than males and leave the males to raise the chicks.

name: Common Murre
entry: It nests shoulder to shoulder on bare cliff ledges. Its pointed eggs spin in a circle instead of rolling off. Before they can fly, chicks leap off the cliffs to the sea, where their fathers raise them.

name: Northern Fulmar
entry: It defends its nest by spitting a stinking stomach oil at intruders. The oil can mat the feathers of attacking birds so badly they cannot fly. Fulmars can live over 40 years.

name: Dickinsonia
range: Ediacaran, 558 million years ago · Australia & Russia
entry: This flat, ribbed oval lived before almost any other animal. For decades no one knew if it was a lichen, fungus or animal, until scientists found traces of animal cholesterol preserved in one of its fossils.

name: Anomalocaris
range: Cambrian, 508 million years ago · Burgess Shale, Canada
entry: It was one of the first big predators, grabbing prey with two spiny front arms. Its parts were first found separately and thought to be a shrimp, a jellyfish and a sea cucumber before scientists realized they were one animal.

name: Opabinia
range: Cambrian, 508 million years ago · Burgess Shale, Canada
entry: It had five eyes on stalks and a long, flexible nozzle with a claw at the end. When it was first presented at a scientific meeting, the audience laughed, thinking it was a joke.

name: Hallucigenia
range: Cambrian, 508 million years ago · Burgess Shale, Canada
entry: Its name comes from hallucination because it looked so strange. Scientists first drew it upside down and backward, walking on its spikes. It is related to today's velvet worms.

name: Pikaia
range: Cambrian, 508 million years ago · Burgess Shale, Canada
entry: This small, eel-like swimmer had a flexible rod along its back, the same feature that became the backbone in fish and people. It is one of the earliest known relatives of animals with backbones.

name: Jaekelopterus
entry: It is the largest known arthropod ever, a sea scorpion about eight feet long. A fossil claw 18 inches long revealed its size. Sea scorpions are distant relatives of spiders and horseshoe crabs.

name: Cooksonia
entry: This tiny plant was just a few forked stems topped with spore capsules, with no leaves or roots. It is one of the earliest known plants with tubes to carry water, the plumbing that let plants grow tall.

name: Prototaxites
entry: It towered up to 26 feet tall at a time when most plants were only knee-high. For over a century, scientists debated whether it was a tree, alga or giant fungus. Recent studies suggest it may be a group of life no longer alive today.

name: Dunkleosteus
range: Devonian, 382–358 million years ago · North America & Morocco
entry: This armored fish had no teeth. Instead, its jaws were lined with bony blades that sharpened themselves as they ground together, giving it one of the strongest bites of any fish.

name: Archaeopteris
entry: It was one of the first true trees, with woody trunks up to 30 feet tall. Its spread created the first forests, which changed Earth's air and soil and may have helped cause an ocean extinction.

name: Tiktaalik
range: Late Devonian, 375 million years ago · Arctic Canada
entry: This fish had a neck, strong fins with wrist-like bones, and lungs. Scientists predicted where to find a fish like it and went to the Canadian Arctic to look. After six years, they found it in 2004.

name: Acanthostega
range: Late Devonian, 365 million years ago · Greenland
entry: It had legs with eight fingers on each hand, but it still had gills and lived mostly in water. Its legs were probably used to push through weedy swamps rather than walk on land.

name: Ichthyostega
range: Late Devonian, 365 million years ago · Greenland
entry: It was one of the first backboned animals able to haul itself onto land, dragging its body forward with strong front legs like a seal. It still had a fish-like tail and spent much of its time in water.

name: Meganeura
entry: This relative of dragonflies had wings over two feet across, one of the largest flying insects ever. Some scientists think higher oxygen levels in the air at the time let insects grow so big.

name: Arthropleura
range: Carboniferous–Permian, 345–290 million years ago · North America & Europe
entry: It was the largest land invertebrate ever, a millipede up to eight feet long. Its fossil trackways show it roamed the swampy coal forests. In 2024, a fossil revealed its head, which had eyes like a crustacean's.

name: Lepidodendron
entry: This tree grew up to 130 feet tall and had bark covered in diamond-shaped scars that look like reptile scales. Its buried remains became much of the coal that powered the Industrial Revolution.

name: Tully Monster
entry: It had eyes on a sideways bar and a long snout ending in a tiny toothed claw. Scientists still argue about whether it was a fish, a mollusk or something else. It is the state fossil of Illinois.

name: Hylonomus
range: Carboniferous, 312 million years ago · Nova Scotia, Canada
entry: This small, lizard-like animal is one of the oldest known reptiles. Its fossils were found inside the hollow stumps of fossil trees, where it may have hunted insects or gotten trapped.

name: Dimetrodon
range: Permian, 295–272 million years ago · North America & Germany
entry: It is often mistaken for a dinosaur, but it lived 40 million years before the first dinosaurs and was more closely related to mammals. Its tall back sail may have helped control its body heat.

name: Inostrancevia
range: Permian, 260–252 million years ago · Russia & South Africa
entry: This mammal relative was a top predator with saber-like fangs up to six inches long. It hunted just before the Great Dying, the worst mass extinction in Earth's history.

name: Lystrosaurus
entry: This stocky, tusked plant-eater survived the Great Dying, when about 90% of ocean species died out. Afterward, it was so common that it made up most land animals in some areas.

name: Glossopteris
range: Permian, 299–252 million years ago · Africa, South America, India, Australia & Antarctica
entry: Its fossil leaves are found on continents now separated by oceans. This helped prove that the continents were once joined together in a giant landmass called Gondwana.

name: Coelurosauravus
range: Permian, 260 million years ago · Germany & Madagascar
entry: It was one of the first backboned animals to glide. It spread wings made of skin stretched over rods that grew from its body, not from its ribs or arms, a design no living animal has.

name: Scutosaurus
entry: This barrel-bodied plant-eater was covered in bony plates and had a spiky face. It may have made loud calls using its throat, like a frog. It lived in dry floodplains just before the Great Dying.

name: Coelophysis
range: Late Triassic, 210 million years ago · New Mexico
entry: This slim, fast early dinosaur had hollow bones like a bird. Hundreds were found together at Ghost Ranch in New Mexico. A skull of one went to space aboard the shuttle Endeavour in 1998.

name: Plateosaurus
range: Late Triassic, 214–204 million years ago · Europe
entry: It was one of the first big plant-eating dinosaurs, walking on two legs with grasping hands. Many were found stuck in mud where they sank, and it is one of the best-known dinosaurs in Europe.

name: Archaeopteryx
range: Late Jurassic, 150 million years ago · Germany
entry: It had feathers and wings like a bird, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like a dinosaur. Found in 1861, just after Darwin's On the Origin of Species, it became famous evidence for evolution.

name: Brontosaurus
range: Late Jurassic, 156–146 million years ago · western United States
entry: Its name means thunder lizard. For about a century, scientists thought it was the same animal as Apatosaurus and dropped the name. In 2015, a detailed study showed it was different, and Brontosaurus was brought back.

name: Brachiosaurus
range: Late Jurassic, 154–150 million years ago · western United States
entry: Its front legs were longer than its back legs, so it stood tall like a giraffe and could reach leaves about 40 feet up. It was one of the tallest dinosaurs known.

name: Stegosaurus
range: Late Jurassic, 155–145 million years ago · western United States & Portugal
entry: It had tall plates along its back and four long spikes on its tail, called a thagomizer. A fossil Allosaurus has a wound that matches a Stegosaurus spike. Its brain was tiny for such a huge animal.

name: Allosaurus
range: Late Jurassic, 155–145 million years ago · western United States & Portugal
entry: It was the top predator of its time, about 30 feet long. Its skull was light and flexible, and it may have attacked by slashing with its upper jaw like a hatchet. One famous skeleton, Big Al, had many healed injuries.

name: Dilophosaurus
range: Early Jurassic, 193 million years ago · Arizona
entry: It had two thin, bony crests on its head. The movie Jurassic Park gave it a neck frill and venom spit, but there is no evidence it had either. It was actually about 20 feet long, much bigger than the movie version.

name: Liopleurodon
range: Middle Jurassic, 166–160 million years ago · Europe
entry: This short-necked marine reptile, a pliosaur, was a top ocean predator with a huge head and teeth. It may have smelled prey underwater by passing water through its nostrils.

name: Ichthyosaurus
range: Early Jurassic, 200–190 million years ago · England & Germany
entry: It looked like a dolphin but was a reptile, and it gave birth to live young in the water. Fossil hunter Mary Anning and her brother found one of the first complete skeletons in England in the early 1800s.

name: Rhamphorhynchus
range: Late Jurassic, 150 million years ago · Germany
entry: This flying reptile had needle-like teeth for catching fish and a long tail ending in a diamond-shaped vane. One fossil shows it caught in the jaws of a large fish, which had in turn caught it.

name: Compsognathus
range: Late Jurassic, 150 million years ago · Germany & France
entry: It was one of the smallest known dinosaurs, about the size of a turkey. A fossil was found with a lizard in its stomach, showing it hunted small, fast prey.

name: Ammonite
range: Devonian to Late Cretaceous, 400–66 million years ago · worldwide
entry: These relatives of octopuses lived in coiled, chambered shells and filled the seas for over 300 million years. Some grew over six feet across. They vanished with the non-bird dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

name: Yi qi
range: Late Jurassic, 160 million years ago · China
entry: This small, feathered dinosaur had wings made of skin stretched between a long rod-like bone and its fingers, like a bat. Its name means strange wing, and it was one of the shortest names given to any dinosaur.

name: Anchiornis
range: Late Jurassic, 160 million years ago · China
entry: It was the first dinosaur whose full colors were worked out, by studying tiny pigment structures in its fossil feathers. It was gray and black with a red crest and black-and-white wings, like a modern bird.

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
range: Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago · western North America
entry: It had one of the strongest bites of any land animal, able to crush bone. Its arms were short but very muscular. The famous skeleton named Sue is over 40 feet long and shows many healed injuries.

name: Triceratops
range: Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago · western North America
entry: It had three horns and a huge bony frill. Fossils show wounds from both T. rex bites and fights with other Triceratops, where horns locked together. It lived right up until the asteroid impact.

name: Velociraptor
range: Late Cretaceous, 75–71 million years ago · Mongolia & China
entry: The real Velociraptor was about the size of a turkey and covered in feathers, unlike the movies. It had a large sickle claw on each foot. One fossil shows it locked in battle with a Protoceratops.

name: Spinosaurus
range: Cretaceous, 99–93 million years ago · North Africa
entry: It may have been the longest meat-eating dinosaur, with a tall sail on its back and a snout like a crocodile's. A paddle-shaped tail found in 2020 suggests it spent much of its time in rivers hunting fish.

name: Ankylosaurus
range: Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago · western North America
entry: It was covered in bony armor plates, even over its eyelids. Its heavy tail club could swing hard enough to break bones. It lived alongside T. rex and Triceratops.

name: Borealopelta
range: Early Cretaceous, 112 million years ago · Alberta, Canada
entry: It is so well preserved, with armor, skin and even stomach contents, that it looks like a stone statue. Its coloring shows it was reddish on top and lighter underneath, meaning even this huge armored dinosaur needed camouflage.

name: Pachycephalosaurus
range: Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago · western North America
entry: Its skull had a dome of solid bone up to ten inches thick. Healed injuries on some skulls suggest they really did head-butt each other, perhaps in contests over mates.

name: Parasaurolophus
range: Late Cretaceous, 77–73 million years ago · western North America
entry: It had a long, hollow crest curving back from its head. Air passages inside the crest may have worked like a trombone, letting it make deep calls. Scientists built a model and heard a low, eerie sound.

name: Iguanodon
range: Early Cretaceous, 126–122 million years ago · Europe
entry: It was one of the first dinosaurs ever named, in 1825. Early scientists thought its thumb spike was a horn on its nose. In 1878, miners in Belgium found dozens of complete skeletons.

name: Argentinosaurus
range: Late Cretaceous, 94 million years ago · Argentina
entry: It may have been the largest land animal that ever lived, over 100 feet long and weighing as much as 15 elephants. Its backbones alone are taller than a person.

name: Therizinosaurus
range: Late Cretaceous, 70 million years ago · Mongolia
entry: It had claws up to three feet long, the longest of any known animal. When first found, the claws were thought to belong to a giant turtle. Despite the claws, it was probably a plant-eater that used them to pull down branches.

name: Microraptor
range: Early Cretaceous, 120 million years ago · China
entry: It had long feathers on both its arms and legs, like four wings. Pigment in its fossil feathers shows it was glossy black with a shimmering blue sheen, like a crow.

name: Quetzalcoatlus
range: Late Cretaceous, 68–66 million years ago · Texas
entry: It was one of the largest flying animals ever, with wings about 35 feet across and standing as tall as a giraffe. It likely stalked small animals on the ground like a stork and could launch into the air using its arms.

name: Pteranodon
range: Late Cretaceous, 86–84 million years ago · central North America
entry: This flying reptile had a wingspan over 20 feet and no teeth, catching fish like a pelican. Males had much larger head crests than females. It was not a dinosaur, but a close relative.

name: Mosasaurus
range: Late Cretaceous, 82–66 million years ago · worldwide seas
entry: This giant sea lizard was related to monitor lizards and snakes. It had a second row of teeth on the roof of its mouth to grip prey. Its skull, found in a Dutch quarry in the 1760s, was one of the first fossils recognized as an extinct animal.

name: Elasmosaurus
range: Late Cretaceous, 80 million years ago · Kansas
entry: Its neck had 72 bones, more than any other animal. When the first skeleton was put together in 1868, a scientist placed the head on the end of the tail by mistake, a blunder that sparked a famous feud.

name: Archelon
range: Late Cretaceous, 80 million years ago · South Dakota
entry: It was the largest turtle ever found, over 15 feet long. Its shell was a framework of bone covered in leathery skin, like a leatherback's. It likely ate jellyfish and squid.

name: Sarcosuchus
range: Early Cretaceous, 112 million years ago · Niger & Brazil
entry: Nicknamed SuperCroc, it was about 40 feet long, twice the size of the largest crocodiles today. A strange bulb on the tip of its snout may have been used to make sounds or attract mates.

name: Oviraptor
range: Late Cretaceous, 75 million years ago · Mongolia
entry: Its name means egg thief, because it was found on top of a nest of eggs and scientists thought it was stealing them. Later finds showed the eggs were its own, and it had died protecting them.

name: Maiasaura
range: Late Cretaceous, 76 million years ago · Montana
entry: Its name means good mother lizard. Fossil nests with babies of different sizes show the parents cared for their young after hatching. It is the state fossil of Montana, and one went to space in 1985.

name: Carnotaurus
range: Late Cretaceous, 72–69 million years ago · Argentina
entry: This predator had two short horns over its eyes like a bull and arms even tinier than a T. rex's. Its skin impressions show rows of bumpy scales. Its strong tail muscles may have made it one of the fastest big predators.

name: Nigersaurus
range: Early Cretaceous, 115 million years ago · Niger
entry: Its wide, square mouth held over 500 teeth, and each worn tooth was replaced in as little as two weeks. It held its head low to graze on ferns like a living lawnmower.

name: Protoceratops
range: Late Cretaceous, 75–71 million years ago · Mongolia & China
entry: This sheep-sized plant-eater had a beak and a bony frill. Some historians think ancient gold miners who found its skeletons in the Gobi Desert inspired the legend of the griffin.

name: Troodon
range: Late Cretaceous, 77 million years ago · western North America
entry: It had one of the largest brains for its body size of any dinosaur, plus large, forward-facing eyes that may have helped it hunt at night. It laid eggs in pairs, like some birds.

name: Sinosauropteryx
range: Early Cretaceous, 124 million years ago · China
entry: It was the first dinosaur found with feather-like fuzz, in 1996. Pigment in its fossil shows it was ginger-brown with a striped tail and a dark mask across its eyes, like a raccoon.

name: Tupandactylus
range: Early Cretaceous, 112 million years ago · Brazil
entry: This pterosaur had a gigantic sail-shaped crest on its head, much bigger than the rest of its skull. A fossil found in 2022 showed its crest and head were covered in fuzzy, feather-like fibers.

name: Archaefructus
range: Early Cretaceous, 125 million years ago · China
entry: It is one of the oldest known flowering plants. It had no petals and grew in lakes, with seeds held in tiny pods along its stems. Flowering plants later spread to cover most of the world.

name: Petrified Forest Tree
range: Late Triassic, 225 million years ago · Arizona
entry: Giant conifer logs were buried by volcanic ash and river mud, and over millions of years minerals replaced the wood with rainbow-colored quartz. The logs in Petrified Forest National Park are now solid stone.

name: Helicoprion
entry: For a century, scientists puzzled over its fossil: a spiral of teeth like a buzzsaw. A 2013 scan showed the whorl sat in its lower jaw and slid backward to slice squid. It was related to today's ratfish.

name: Leedsichthys
range: Middle Jurassic, 165 million years ago · Europe & Chile
entry: It may be the largest bony fish that ever lived, possibly over 50 feet long. Like today's whale sharks, it was a gentle filter feeder that strained tiny animals from the water.

name: Pakicetus
entry: This wolf-sized animal lived on land and waded in streams. It looks nothing like a whale, but its ear bones have a special shape found only in whales, marking it as one of their earliest ancestors.

name: Ambulocetus
entry: Its name means walking, swimming whale. It had big webbed feet and lived like a crocodile, lurking in shallow water to ambush animals that came to drink.

name: Basilosaurus
range: Eocene, 40–34 million years ago · worldwide seas
entry: This fully ocean-living whale was up to 60 feet long, with a snake-like body. It still had tiny back legs a few inches long, left over from its land ancestors. Its name means king lizard because it was first mistaken for a reptile.

name: Eohippus
range: Eocene, 55–45 million years ago · North America
entry: The earliest horses were about the size of a fox. It had four toes on its front feet and three on its back feet, and it browsed on soft leaves in forests.

name: Mesohippus
range: Oligocene, 37–32 million years ago · North America
entry: It was the size of a sheep, with three toes on each foot. As forests gave way to open woodlands, horses like it grew longer legs for running.

name: Merychippus
range: Miocene, 17–10 million years ago · North America
entry: It lived in herds on the spreading grasslands. It stood on a single large middle toe, and its tall, tough teeth could grind gritty grass, much like modern horses.

name: Titanoboa
entry: It is the largest snake ever found, over 40 feet long and as heavy as a small car. It lived in hot rainforest swamps soon after the dinosaurs died out and probably ate giant turtles and crocodile relatives.

name: Gastornis
range: Paleocene–Eocene, 56–45 million years ago · Europe, North America & Asia
entry: This huge flightless bird stood almost seven feet tall with a massive beak. It was once imagined as a fierce predator, but chemical studies of its bones suggest it mostly ate plants, seeds and nuts.

name: Terror Bird
range: Pliocene, 5–2 million years ago · Florida & Texas
entry: This flightless predator stood over six feet tall with a hooked beak like an axe. Terror birds ruled South America for millions of years, and this one crossed into North America when the continents joined.

name: Megalodon
range: Miocene–Pliocene, 23–3.6 million years ago · worldwide seas
entry: It was the largest predatory shark ever, possibly over 50 feet long, with teeth as big as a hand. It was warm-bodied and hunted whales. It is known mostly from its teeth, which are common fossils.

name: Livyatan
entry: This giant sperm whale had the largest teeth of any animal that uses them to eat, over a foot long. It hunted other whales and may have competed with Megalodon. Its name honors Herman Melville, author of Moby-Dick.

name: Entelodon
range: Eocene–Oligocene, 37–28 million years ago · Europe & Asia
entry: Nicknamed the hell pig, it looked like a giant warthog with bony knobs on its face and powerful jaws. It was actually more closely related to hippos and whales than to pigs, and it ate almost anything.

name: Paraceratherium
range: Oligocene, 34–23 million years ago · Central Asia
entry: It was one of the largest land mammals ever, a hornless rhino relative about 16 feet tall at the shoulder. It browsed on treetops like a giraffe and weighed as much as several elephants.

name: Smilodon
range: Pleistocene, 2.5 million–10,000 years ago · the Americas
entry: Its saber-shaped fangs were up to 11 inches long. It ambushed large prey and held it with strong forelimbs. Thousands of its bones were found trapped in the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles.

name: Megatherium
range: Pleistocene, 5 million–12,000 years ago · South America
entry: This ground sloth was as big as an elephant and could rear up on its hind legs to reach leaves 12 feet high. Charles Darwin collected its fossils on his voyage on the Beagle.

name: Glyptodon
range: Pleistocene, 2.5 million–12,000 years ago · South America
entry: This giant relative of armadillos was the size of a small car and wore a domed shell made of over 1,000 bony plates. Early people in South America may have used its shells as shelters.

name: Woolly Rhinoceros
range: Pleistocene, 350,000–14,000 years ago · Europe & northern Asia
entry: It had a thick woolly coat and a long front horn it may have swept through snow to reach grass. Ice Age people painted it on cave walls, and frozen carcasses have been found in Siberian permafrost.

name: Irish Elk
entry: This giant deer had the largest antlers of any known deer, up to 12 feet across. Despite its name, it was not an elk and lived far beyond Ireland, though many skeletons were found in Irish bogs.

name: Cave Bear
entry: This big bear hibernated in caves, and many died there over the winters, leaving caves filled with thousands of bones. Despite its size, its teeth show it ate mostly plants.

name: Diprotodon
entry: It was the largest marsupial ever, a wombat relative the size of a rhinoceros. Like wombats, the mother carried her baby in a backward-facing pouch. It lived alongside the first people in Australia.

name: Megalania
entry: This giant relative of the Komodo dragon was one of the largest land lizards ever, perhaps over 20 feet long. Like its living cousins, it may have had a venomous bite.

name: Thylacoleo
entry: This marsupial predator had the strongest bite for its size of any known mammal, with blade-like teeth for slicing. It had a large, hooked thumb claw and could climb trees.

name: Procoptodon
entry: It was the largest kangaroo ever, about 6.5 feet tall, with a short, flat face. It may have walked on two legs instead of hopping and used long, clawed fingers to pull down branches.

name: Giant Moa
range: Holocene, until about 1400 CE · New Zealand
entry: Females of this flightless bird could stand over 11 feet tall with necks stretched up. It had no wings at all. Moa were hunted to extinction within about 200 years of people arriving in New Zealand.

name: Haast's Eagle
range: Holocene, until about 1400 CE · New Zealand
entry: It was the largest eagle ever known, with talons as big as a tiger's claws. It hunted moa many times its own weight. When people wiped out the moa, the eagle vanished too.

name: Elephant Bird
range: Holocene, until about 1,000 years ago · Madagascar
entry: This flightless bird was one of the heaviest birds ever, and it laid the largest known eggs, holding as much as 150 chicken eggs. Its closest living relative is New Zealand's tiny kiwi.

name: Dodo
entry: This flightless pigeon lived on the island of Mauritius with no predators. It vanished within a century of sailors arriving, killed by people and the rats, pigs and monkeys they brought. As dead as a dodo became a saying.

name: Great Auk
entry: This flightless seabird was the original penguin, and penguins in the Southern Hemisphere were named after it. It was hunted for feathers and meat, and the last known pair was killed in Iceland in 1844.

name: Passenger Pigeon
entry: It may have been the most numerous bird in the world, with flocks of billions that darkened the sky for hours. Mass hunting wiped it out in a few decades. The last one, Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914.

name: Carolina Parakeet
entry: It was the only parrot native to the eastern United States. It ate toxic cocklebur seeds, and cats that ate the birds reportedly died. The last known one died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1918, in the same cage as Martha.

name: Quagga
entry: This zebra had stripes only on its front half, fading to plain brown behind. The last one died in an Amsterdam zoo in 1883. It was the first extinct animal to have its DNA studied, in 1984.

name: Aurochs
range: Holocene, until 1627 · Europe, Asia & North Africa
entry: It was the wild ancestor of all domestic cattle, much larger than modern cows, with huge curved horns. Ice Age people painted it on cave walls. The last known aurochs died in a Polish forest in 1627.

name: Huia
entry: Males had short, strong beaks for chiseling into wood, while females had long, curved beaks for probing for grubs. Its tail feathers were so prized that one sold for a record price at auction in 2010.

name: Golden Toad
range: Holocene, last seen 1989 · Monteverde, Costa Rica
entry: Males were a brilliant orange-gold. Every spring, they gathered in small puddles in one cloud forest. In 1987, over 1,500 were counted. In 1989, only one male was seen, and it has never been found again.

name: Pyrenean Ibex
entry: The last one, Celia, died in 2000. In 2003, scientists cloned her, and a baby ibex was born. It lived only seven minutes, making it the first animal to go extinct twice.

name: Bramble Cay Melomys
range: Holocene, until about 2009 · Bramble Cay, Australia
entry: This small rodent lived only on one tiny sand island in the Great Barrier Reef. Rising seas and storm surges destroyed its habitat. It is considered the first mammal to go extinct because of human-caused climate change.

name: Western Black Rhinoceros
range: Holocene, declared extinct 2011 · West & Central Africa
entry: This subspecies of black rhino was hunted for its horns until none were left. It was declared extinct in 2011. Other black rhino subspecies survive thanks to strict protection.

name: Gigantopithecus
range: Pleistocene, 2 million–300,000 years ago · southern China
entry: This giant ape may have stood nearly ten feet tall. It is known mostly from teeth, first found for sale in Chinese medicine shops as dragon bones. It may have died out when forests shrank.

name: Meiolania
range: Pleistocene, until about 100,000 years ago · Lord Howe Island, Australia
entry: This car-sized land turtle had cow-like horns on its head and a spiked, club-like tail. It could not pull its head into its shell. Its relatives survived on Pacific islands until only about 3,000 years ago.

name: Deinotherium
range: Miocene–Pleistocene, 10 million–1 million years ago · Europe, Africa & Asia
entry: This relative of elephants was one of the largest land mammals ever. Its tusks grew from its lower jaw and curved downward and backward, perhaps for stripping bark or digging roots.

name: Platybelodon
range: Miocene, 15–4 million years ago · Asia & Africa
entry: This elephant relative had flat, shovel-like lower tusks. It was once thought to scoop water plants, but wear on its tusks suggests it used them like scissors to cut branches.

name: Arsinoitherium
range: Eocene–Oligocene, 36–30 million years ago · North Africa
entry: It looked like a rhino but had two huge, hollow horns side by side over its nose. Its closest living relatives are elephants and manatees. It lived in swampy forests in what is now Egypt.

name: Chalicotherium
range: Miocene, 15–5 million years ago · Europe, Asia & Africa
entry: This relative of horses had long arms with big claws instead of hooves. It walked on its knuckles like a gorilla and used its claws to pull down branches.

name: Pelagornis
range: Oligocene, 25 million years ago · South Carolina
entry: This seabird had the largest wingspan of any known flying bird, over 20 feet. It had no real teeth, but its beak was lined with sharp, tooth-like bony spikes for gripping slippery fish and squid.

name: Macrauchenia
range: Pleistocene, 7 million–10,000 years ago · South America
entry: It had a camel-like body, long neck and nostrils high on its head that may have held a short trunk. Darwin found its bones and was puzzled by it. Ancient proteins later showed it was related to horses and rhinos.

name: American Mastodon
range: Pleistocene, until about 11,000 years ago · North America
entry: It looked like a mammoth but belonged to a different branch of the elephant family and ate twigs and leaves in forests. Its fossils sparked early debates about extinction, and Thomas Jefferson hoped living ones would be found.

name: Dire Wolf
entry: It was bigger and heavier than a gray wolf, with a stronger bite. Over 4,000 were found trapped in the La Brea Tar Pits. DNA showed in 2021 that it was not a close cousin of gray wolves after all.

name: Giant Beaver
range: Pleistocene, until about 10,000 years ago · North America
entry: This beaver was the size of a black bear, with front teeth up to six inches long. Unlike modern beavers, it probably did not cut down trees or build dams, eating water plants instead.

name: Repenomamus
range: Early Cretaceous, 125 million years ago · China
entry: Most mammals of its time were tiny, but this badger-sized one ate dinosaurs. One fossil was found with a baby Psittacosaurus in its stomach, and another was locked in a fight with one.

name: Xerces Blue
range: Holocene, until about 1943 · San Francisco, California
entry: This small blue butterfly lived only in the sand dunes of San Francisco. As the city grew over its habitat, it disappeared. It is thought to be the first American butterfly to go extinct because of people.

name: Rocky Mountain Locust
entry: In 1875, a swarm of this locust covered an area bigger than California, perhaps the largest swarm of animals ever recorded. Just 27 years later, it was gone, likely because farming destroyed the river valleys where it laid eggs.

name: Kauaʻi ʻŌʻō
entry: This Hawaiian honeyeater was known for its flute-like song. A recording from 1975 captures a lone male singing a duet song and pausing for a female's reply that never came. The species was last heard in 1987.

name: Stephens Island Wren
range: Holocene, until 1895 · Stephens Island, New Zealand
entry: This tiny, nearly flightless wren scurried around like a mouse. When a lighthouse was built on its island, cats arrived with the keepers, and the wren was wiped out within a year or two.

name: Silphium
range: Ancient, until about the 1st century CE · Cyrene, Libya
entry: This plant was one of the most prized spices and medicines of the ancient Greeks and Romans, worth its weight in silver. It grew only near the city of Cyrene and was harvested until it disappeared.

name: Southern Mammoth
range: Pleistocene, 2.5–0.8 million years ago · Europe & Asia
entry: This early mammoth lived in warm, wooded areas and had little hair. It was taller than any living elephant. As the climate cooled, its descendants spread into open grasslands.

name: Steppe Mammoth
range: Pleistocene, 1.7–0.2 million years ago · Europe & Asia
entry: This was one of the largest mammoths, living on cold, open grasslands. In 2021, DNA over a million years old was read from its teeth, the oldest DNA ever sequenced at the time.

name: Woolly Mammoth
range: Pleistocene–Holocene, 300,000–4,000 years ago · northern Eurasia & North America
entry: It was covered in shaggy fur with small ears and a short tail to save heat. Frozen mammoths with skin and hair have been found in Siberia. The last ones lived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, after the Egyptian pyramids were built.

name: Deinosuchus
range: Late Cretaceous, 82–75 million years ago · North America
entry: This giant alligator relative grew over 30 feet long. Bite marks on dinosaur bones show it ambushed dinosaurs at the water's edge. Its teeth were thick and blunt for crushing turtles.

name: Utahraptor
range: Early Cretaceous, 135 million years ago · Utah
entry: It was the largest known raptor dinosaur, about 20 feet long, with a nine-inch sickle claw on each foot. A huge block of stone in Utah holds several Utahraptors of different ages, possibly trapped together in quicksand.

name: Psittacosaurus
range: Early Cretaceous, 125–100 million years ago · Asia
entry: This small plant-eater had a parrot-like beak and bristles on its tail. One fossil preserved its colors, showing it was dark on top and pale below, a camouflage pattern that suggests it lived in shady forests.

name: Baryonyx
range: Early Cretaceous, 130–125 million years ago · England
entry: It was discovered by an amateur fossil hunter who found a huge claw in a clay pit in 1983. Fish scales were found in its stomach, the first direct proof that some dinosaurs ate fish.

name: Deinocheirus
range: Late Cretaceous, 70 million years ago · Mongolia
entry: For almost 50 years, it was known only from a pair of eight-foot arms. When full skeletons were finally found in 2014, it turned out to have a hump, a duck-like bill and a belly full of fish and plants.

name: Megacerops
range: Eocene, 38–34 million years ago · North America
entry: This rhino-like giant had a Y-shaped horn on its nose. The Lakota people found its bones and called it thunder horse, believing it caused thunderstorms. Its scientific relatives are called brontotheres, thunder beasts.

name: Dictyostelium Amoeba
entry: It lives as a single cell in the soil, hunting bacteria. When food runs out, starving cells release a chemical signal, and up to 100,000 of them stream together toward the source.

name: Dictyostelium Slug
entry: The gathered cells form a tiny slug about the size of a grain of sand. It crawls toward light and warmth as a single body, searching for a good place to release spores.

name: Dictyostelium Fruiting Body
entry: About a fifth of the cells die to build a stalk, lifting the rest up as a ball of spores. Scientists study this sacrifice to understand how cooperation evolved.

name: Tardigrade
entry: This eight-legged water bear is a predator that hunts rotifers and other tiny animals in the water film on moss. In 2007, tardigrades were sent into open space and some survived.

name: Tardigrade Tun
entry: When its home dries out, it pulls in its legs, loses almost all its water and becomes a lifeless-looking barrel called a tun. In this state it can survive freezing, boiling, crushing pressure and years without water.

name: Escherichia coli
entry: It is the most studied living thing on Earth. Most strains are harmless and live in your gut, helping make vitamin K. In good conditions, one cell can divide every 20 minutes.

name: Staphylococcus aureus
entry: About a third of people carry it harmlessly in their nose. Its clusters look like golden bunches of grapes. Some strains, called MRSA, resist many antibiotics.

name: Streptococcus pyogenes
entry: Its round cells grow in chains like strings of beads. It causes strep throat and scarlet fever, and in rare cases a fast-spreading infection called flesh-eating disease.

name: Conan the Bacterium
entry: It survives radiation doses about a thousand times higher than would kill a human by rapidly rebuilding its shattered DNA. In an experiment, colonies survived three years on the outside of the International Space Station.

name: Hay Bacillus
entry: When times get hard, it forms a tough spore that can survive for years. It ferments soybeans into natto, a sticky Japanese food. Its gooey strings are made of a chemical it releases.

name: Botulinum Bacterium
entry: It makes botulinum toxin, the most poisonous substance known. A tiny amount can paralyze. Doctors inject even tinier doses, called Botox, to relax muscles and smooth wrinkles.

name: Helicobacter pylori
entry: It corkscrews into the lining of the stomach and neutralizes acid around itself. To prove it caused ulcers, doctor Barry Marshall drank a flask of it and got sick. He later won a Nobel Prize.

name: Yogurt Bacterium
entry: It turns the sugar in milk into lactic acid, which thickens it into yogurt. It is named after Bulgaria, where a scientist found it in traditional yogurt in 1905.

name: Streptomyces griseus
entry: It grows in branching threads like a fungus. It gave us streptomycin, the first antibiotic to treat tuberculosis. Its relatives make geosmin, the earthy smell you notice after rain.

name: Rhizobium
entry: It lives inside pink nodules on the roots of peas and beans and turns nitrogen from the air into fertilizer for the plant. In return, the plant feeds it sugar.

name: Wolbachia
entry: It may infect about half of all insect species. It spreads through eggs and can kill males or turn them into females. Mosquitoes carrying it cannot spread dengue well, so scientists release them to fight the disease.

name: Thermus aquaticus
range: Hot springs, first found in Yellowstone
entry: It was discovered in a Yellowstone hot spring in 1966. An enzyme from it, Taq, keeps working near boiling. It made possible PCR, the method used to copy DNA in labs, including COVID tests.

name: Magnetospirillum
entry: It builds a chain of tiny magnetic crystals inside its body that works like a compass needle. It lines up with Earth's magnetic field to swim down toward the low-oxygen mud it prefers.

name: Geobacter
entry: It grows hair-like protein nanowires that conduct electricity, passing electrons to rust and other minerals. Scientists use it to build batteries that make power from mud.

name: Cable Bacteria
entry: Thousands of cells join end to end into chains over an inch long, running up and down through the mud like power cables. They carry an electric current from deep mud to the oxygen near the surface.

name: Wolf-pack Bacterium
entry: It hunts in swarms like a wolf pack, surrounding other bacteria and dissolving them with chemicals. When food runs out, thousands gather to build a fruiting body full of spores.

name: Bdellovibrio
entry: It is one of the fastest swimmers for its size, reaching about 100 body lengths per second. It rams into other bacteria, bores inside and eats them from within before bursting out.

name: Thiomargarita magnifica
entry: Discovered in 2022, this bacterium can grow nearly an inch long, big enough to see with your eyes. That is like a human the size of Mount Everest. It lives on sulfur in Caribbean mangroves.

name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
entry: It makes a blue-green pigment that glows under ultraviolet light and smells faintly like grapes. It forms slimy biofilms that shield it from antibiotics, making it a dangerous hospital infection.

name: Star Jelly
entry: This cyanobacterium lives in colonies that dry into black crusts. After rain, they swell into jelly blobs overnight, and people once believed they fell from shooting stars. It is eaten as a delicacy in China.

name: Salmonella
entry: It is a common cause of food poisoning from undercooked eggs and chicken. One type causes typhoid fever. A cook known as Typhoid Mary carried it without getting sick and infected dozens of people in the early 1900s.

name: Listeria
entry: Unlike most germs, it keeps growing in the cold of a refrigerator. Inside a cell, it hijacks the cell's scaffolding to build a comet-like tail that rockets it into neighboring cells.

name: Lyme Spirochete
range: Ticks & mice of North America & Europe
entry: This long, spiral bacterium spreads through tick bites and causes Lyme disease. It twists like a corkscrew through skin and joints. The disease is named after Lyme, Connecticut, where it was identified in the 1970s.

name: Swiss Cheese Bacterium
entry: It eats lactic acid in aging cheese and releases carbon dioxide gas. The bubbles get trapped and become the famous holes, called eyes, in Swiss cheese. It also gives the cheese its nutty flavor.

name: Vinegar Bacterium
entry: It turns alcohol into acetic acid, the sour part of vinegar. It forms a slimy film called the mother of vinegar, which can be used to start new batches.

name: SAR11
entry: This tiny bacterium may be the most abundant living thing on Earth. It makes up about a quarter of all cells in the ocean. Its genome is one of the most streamlined of any free-living organism.

name: Salt Pond Archaeon
entry: It needs water many times saltier than the sea. A purple protein in its skin captures sunlight to make energy. Blooms of it turn salt ponds bright pink and red.

name: Methanobrevibacter
entry: It is the most common archaeon in the human gut. It eats hydrogen made by gut bacteria and releases methane gas, helping the bacteria digest food better.

name: Pyrolobus
entry: It grows at temperatures up to 235°F, well above boiling, and stops growing if the water cools below about 194°F. It lives in the walls of black smoker chimneys on the ocean floor.

name: Strain 116
entry: One strain of this archaeon holds the record for the highest temperature at which life can grow: 252°F, under high pressure in a lab. It lives near vents and makes methane.

name: Sulfolobus
entry: It thrives in bubbling volcanic pools that are both near boiling and as acidic as lemon juice. It eats sulfur and was first found in the craters of Italian volcanoes.

name: Square Archaeon
entry: It is shaped like a flat, square postage stamp, one of the only square cells in nature. Tiny gas bubbles inside help it float near the sunny surface of salty ponds.

name: Asgard Archaeon
entry: Its group is the closest living relative of complex cells like ours. It took Japanese scientists 12 years to grow it in the lab. It has long, branching tentacles that may hint at how our ancestors captured bacteria.

name: Nanoarchaeum
entry: It is one of the smallest known cells and has one of the smallest genomes. It cannot live on its own, riding on the surface of a bigger archaeon named Ignicoccus and borrowing its materials.

name: Ignicoccus
entry: Its name means fire ball. It lives in hot vents and plays host to the tiny Nanoarchaeum, which clings to its surface. It has an unusual outer membrane with its own compartment.

name: C. difficile
entry: It waits as tough spores until antibiotics wipe out a person's normal gut bacteria, then takes over and releases toxins. One of the best cures is surprising: a transplant of healthy gut bacteria from a donor.

name: Desulforudis
range: Two miles deep in a South African gold mine
entry: It lives almost two miles underground in water that has been cut off for millions of years, making it an ecosystem of one species. It gets energy from chemicals made when radioactive rocks split water.

name: Bleeding Bread Bacterium
entry: It grows as bright red spots on bread and in bathroom corners. In medieval times, its blood-colored colonies on bread and communion wafers were sometimes taken as miracles.

name: Snowmaker Bacterium
entry: A protein on its surface helps water freeze at warmer temperatures than normal. It damages crops with frost and may help trigger snow and rain in clouds. Ski resorts use it to make artificial snow.

name: Bt Bacterium
entry: It makes crystals of protein that are toxic to caterpillars but harmless to people. Organic farmers spray it on crops, and its genes have been added to some crops so they protect themselves.

name: Agrobacterium
entry: It inserts a piece of its own DNA into plant cells, making them grow a lump called a crown gall. Scientists use this natural trick to add new genes to crop plants.

name: Buchnera
entry: It lives only inside special cells of aphids and makes nutrients missing from plant sap. It has been passed from mother aphid to her young for over 150 million years and can no longer survive on its own.

name: Deep-vent Green Sulfur Bacterium
entry: Green sulfur bacteria can harvest extremely dim light. One relative found at a deep-sea vent seems to photosynthesize using the faint glow of the hot vent itself, with no sunlight at all.

name: Angel's Glow Bacterium
entry: It lives in worms that hunt insects and makes their victims glow. After the Civil War battle of Shiloh, some soldiers' wounds glowed in the dark and healed better. Two teenagers later suggested this bacterium was the cause.

name: Caulobacter
entry: It attaches to surfaces with one of the strongest glues known in nature, stronger for its size than any human-made superglue. Each time it divides, one daughter stays stuck and the other swims away.

name: Streptococcus mutans
entry: It lives in plaque on your teeth and turns sugar into acid, which eats holes in tooth enamel. It is a main cause of cavities, which is why brushing and less candy help.

name: Baby Gut Bacterium
entry: Breast milk contains special sugars that babies cannot digest, but this bacterium can. It is one of the first bacteria to settle in a baby's gut and helps protect against germs.

name: Leprosy Bacterium
entry: It grows extremely slowly, dividing only about every two weeks, and prefers the cooler parts of the body. It is one of the only bacteria that armadillos can catch and carry. Leprosy is curable today.

name: Weizmann's Bacterium
entry: During World War I, chemist Chaim Weizmann used it to make acetone for explosives when supplies ran out. He later became the first president of Israel.

name: Plastic-eating Bacterium
range: Found outside a bottle recycling plant in Japan
entry: It was discovered in 2016 in soil outside a Japanese recycling plant. It can break down PET, the plastic in soda bottles, and use it as food. Scientists are improving its enzymes to recycle plastic.

name: Beggiatoa
entry: It grows in long white threads that form mats on stinky, sulfur-rich mud. In 1887, scientist Sergei Winogradsky used it to discover that some life feeds on chemicals instead of light or food.

name: Mycoplasma genitalium
entry: It has one of the smallest genomes of any cell that can copy itself, with fewer than 600 genes and no cell wall. Scientists have modeled every molecule inside it, and work on it and its relatives led to the first cell with a lab-built genome in 2010.

name: Aquifex
entry: It grows at about 200°F. Its name means water maker, because it combines hydrogen and oxygen to get energy and releases water. It may belong to one of the oldest branches of bacteria.

name: Oil-eating Bacterium
entry: It is usually rare, but after oil spills it multiplies rapidly and eats the oil. It helps clean up spills naturally, and scientists study it to speed cleanups.

name: Typhus Bacterium
entry: Spread by body lice, it caused typhus epidemics that killed millions during wars and famines. It can only live inside other cells. Its relatives may be the ancestors of the mitochondria in our own cells.

name: Vortex Bacterium
entry: Its cells swarm together in rotating whirlpools that sweep across a dish, forming beautiful branching patterns. Groups can even carry other bacteria along with them.

name: Methanosarcina
entry: It makes methane from many foods. Some scientists think a population boom of its ancestors 252 million years ago flooded the oceans and air with gas, helping cause the worst mass extinction in Earth's history.

name: Pyrococcus furiosus
entry: Its name means rushing fireball. It grows best at about 212°F, boiling-water temperature, and can double its numbers in about 37 minutes. Its enzymes are used in labs.

name: Acne Bacterium
entry: It lives deep in skin pores, feeding on oil. It is usually harmless and even protects skin from other germs, but when pores clog, it can help cause pimples.

name: Microcystis
entry: This cyanobacterium forms green blooms that look like pea soup on warm lakes. It makes a liver toxin. In 2014, a bloom in Lake Erie made the tap water of Toledo, Ohio, unsafe for days.

name: Violet Bacterium
entry: It makes a vivid purple pigment called violacein, which turns its colonies deep violet. The pigment protects it from predators and is being studied as a medicine against parasites and cancer.

name: Amoeba
entry: It has no fixed shape. It moves by pushing out finger-like blobs called pseudopods and flows into them. It is named after Proteus, a Greek sea god who could change his shape.

name: Paramecium
entry: This slipper-shaped cell is covered in thousands of tiny beating hairs called cilia. When it bumps into something, it backs up and tries another direction. It can fire tiny harpoons to defend itself.

name: Stentor
entry: This trumpet-shaped cell is big enough to see and colored blue. Cut into pieces, each piece can regrow a whole Stentor. Experiments show it makes decisions, trying different escape moves in order when bothered.

name: Vorticella
entry: This bell-shaped cell sits on a long stalk. When disturbed, the stalk coils up like a spring in milliseconds, one of the fastest movements in the living world.

name: Euglena
entry: It is part plant and part animal. It uses a red eyespot to swim toward light and makes food by photosynthesis, but in the dark it can eat food like an animal.

name: Volvox
entry: It is a hollow ball made of thousands of cells that beat their tails together to roll through the water. Baby colonies grow inside the ball and burst out when they are ready.

name: Optogenetic Alga
entry: It swims toward light using a light-sensitive protein. Scientists put this protein into brain cells so they could switch neurons on and off with light, a technique called optogenetics.

name: Diatom
entry: It lives inside a two-part glass shell with beautiful patterns, like a pillbox. Diatoms make about a fifth of the oxygen on Earth. Their fossil shells are mined as diatomaceous earth.

name: Rock Snot
entry: This diatom grows long stalks that form thick, slimy carpets on riverbeds, which is how it got its unpleasant nickname. Blooms can smother the bottoms of clear, cold streams.

name: Radiolarian
entry: It builds intricate glass skeletons shaped like stars, lanterns and snowflakes. Biologist Ernst Haeckel's drawings of them inspired Art Nouveau design. Their skeletons pile up into sea-floor ooze.

name: Foraminifera
entry: This single cell builds a tiny shell with many chambers. The limestone used for the Great Pyramids of Egypt is packed with fossil shells of an ancient giant foram. Scientists read past climates from their shells.

name: Sleeping Sickness Parasite
range: Tropical Africa, spread by tsetse flies
entry: Every time the immune system learns to spot it, it switches to a new coat of proteins, staying one step ahead. It causes sleeping sickness, which disturbs sleep and can be fatal without treatment.

name: Giardia
entry: Under the microscope, it looks like a smiling face, with two nuclei for eyes. It sticks to the gut with a sucking disc. Hikers catch it from untreated stream water, which is why it is called beaver fever.

name: Toxoplasma
entry: It can only reproduce inside cats. Infected mice and rats lose their fear of cat smell, making them easier to catch. About a third of all people carry it, usually without symptoms.

name: Tetrahymena
entry: It has seven sexes, called mating types, and can mate with any type except its own. Studies of it led to discoveries about the tips of chromosomes and RNA that works like an enzyme, winning two Nobel Prizes.

name: Zooxanthellae
entry: This tiny alga lives inside corals and gives them their colors and most of their food. When the water gets too hot, corals kick it out and turn white, which is called coral bleaching.

name: Dog Vomit Slime Mold
entry: It is a single giant cell that creeps across mulch as a bright yellow blob, looking like scrambled eggs or something a dog left behind. It can soak up zinc and other metals that would poison most living things.

name: Choanoflagellate
entry: It is the closest living relative of animals. When it detects a chemical from certain bacteria, single cells stick together into flower-shaped rosettes, hinting at how the first animals formed.

name: Sun Animalcule
entry: It looks like a tiny sun, with stiff, sticky rays spreading out in all directions. Prey that touches a ray gets stuck and is pulled in and swallowed.

name: Difflugia
entry: This amoeba builds itself a vase-shaped shell by gluing together tiny grains of sand. When it divides, it passes sand grains to its daughter to build a new shell.

name: Didinium
entry: This barrel-shaped hunter harpoons a Paramecium, then swallows it whole, even though its prey is bigger than it is. Their chase is a classic in microscope classes.

name: Tear of the Swan
entry: This teardrop-shaped cell shoots out a neck many times its body length to snatch prey, then folds it back up like origami. Its name means tear of a swan.

name: Spirostomum
entry: This worm-shaped cell is big enough to see. When disturbed, it shrinks to a quarter of its length in a few milliseconds, one of the fastest contractions of any cell, sending out a wave that warns its neighbors.

name: Warnowiid
entry: This single cell has a tiny camera-like eye with a lens and a retina, built from parts of its own cell. It may use it to spot prey. It also fires a harpoon-like structure.

name: Mixotricha
entry: It lives in termite guts and helps them digest wood. It does not swim itself. Instead, hundreds of thousands of spiral bacteria stuck to its surface wiggle together and push it along.

name: Potato Blight
entry: This water mold rots potatoes in the field and in storage. In the 1840s, it destroyed Ireland's potato crops, causing a famine that killed about a million people and forced another million to leave.

name: Micrasterias
entry: This single-celled green alga is shaped like a flat, lacy snowflake. It is made of two perfect mirror-image halves joined in the middle, and when it divides, each half grows a new partner.

name: Haematococcus
entry: When stressed, this green alga fills with a red pigment called astaxanthin and turns blood red. The pigment is fed to farmed salmon to make their flesh pink.

name: Dunaliella
entry: This alga thrives in water saltier than the sea and makes huge amounts of orange beta-carotene. Along with salt-loving archaea, it turns some salt lakes bubblegum pink.

name: Arcella
entry: This amoeba lives in a round, brown shell that looks like a tiny flying saucer. If it gets flipped over, it makes a gas bubble to float and turn itself right side up.

name: Leishmania
entry: This parasite is spread by the bites of tiny sand flies. It hides inside the very immune cells meant to destroy it. It can cause skin sores or damage to internal organs.

name: Hatena
entry: It carries a green alga partner inside it. When it divides, only one daughter keeps the alga and lives like a plant. The other becomes a colorless hunter that must catch a new alga of its own.

name: Gromia
range: Deep sea floor of the Bahamas & Arabian Sea
entry: This single cell is the size of a grape. It slowly rolls or crawls across the sea floor, leaving tracks. Similar tracks in rocks over a billion years old were thought to prove early animals existed, but cells like this could have made them.

name: Paulinella
entry: Almost all plants got their power to photosynthesize from one ancient event. This amoeba captured a cyanobacterium on its own about 100 million years ago, making a second, separate origin of plant-like cells.

name: Mermaid's Wineglass
entry: Each one is a single cell, up to three inches tall, shaped like a tiny umbrella or wineglass. Experiments grafting its caps and stems helped prove that the nucleus holds a cell's instructions.

name: Killer Algae
range: Tropical seas; invasive in the Mediterranean
entry: A whole plant several feet long is a single giant cell with many nuclei. An aquarium strain escaped into the Mediterranean in the 1980s and spread over thousands of acres of sea floor.

name: Baker's Yeast
entry: It eats sugar and releases carbon dioxide and alcohol, making bread rise and beer and wine ferment. In 1996, it became the first complex cell to have its entire genome read.

name: Penicillin Mold
entry: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that this mold had killed the bacteria in one of his dishes. The penicillin it makes became the first widely used antibiotic and has saved many millions of lives.

name: Koji Mold
range: Grown in kitchens & breweries across East Asia
entry: People in Japan and China have grown it on rice and soybeans for thousands of years to make soy sauce, miso and sake. Japan named it its national fungus in 2006.

name: Candida
entry: It lives harmlessly in most people as round yeast cells. When conditions change, it grows long threads that can invade tissue and cause infections like thrush.

name: Chytrid Fungus
entry: It infects the skin of frogs, which they use to breathe and drink. It has driven about 90 amphibian species extinct, the greatest loss of species caused by any known disease.

name: White-nose Fungus
range: Caves of North America, Europe & Asia
entry: It grows only in the cold, on the noses and wings of hibernating bats. The itch wakes the bats too often, and they burn through their fat. It has killed millions of bats in North America since 2006.

name: Black Bread Mold
entry: It spreads across bread in fuzzy gray-white threads topped with tiny black balls full of spores. It sends out runners, like strawberry plants, to reach new food.

name: Noble Rot
entry: It usually ruins fruit as gray mold. But in the right weather on wine grapes, it shrivels them and concentrates their sugar, making rare sweet dessert wines.

name: Hat Thrower Fungus
entry: It grows on dung and aims at the sun. Its bulb bursts and fires its spore cap up to eight feet away, with one of the fastest accelerations in nature, landing on grass that animals will eat.

name: Ergot
entry: It infects rye grains and replaces them with dark, poisonous lumps. Eating it caused outbreaks of a burning disease called St. Anthony's fire. A chemist made LSD from one of its compounds in 1938.

name: Root Fungus Partner
entry: It grows tiny tree-shaped structures inside plant root cells and trades minerals for sugar. Fungi like it partner with most land plants and may have helped plants move onto land 450 million years ago.

name: Radiation-eating Fungus
range: Found inside the ruined Chernobyl reactor & worldwide
entry: Dark fungi like it grow on the walls of the destroyed Chernobyl reactor. Its black pigment, melanin, may help it use radiation for energy. It was grown on the space station to test it as a radiation shield.

name: Orange Bread Mold
entry: This fast-growing orange mold often appears on burned plants after fires. Experiments with it proved that each gene makes one protein, a discovery that won a Nobel Prize in 1958.

name: Nematode-trapping Fungus
entry: When worms are near, it grows sticky loops and snares in the soil. When a worm crawls through a ring, the fungus traps it and grows threads inside to digest it.

name: Candida auris
entry: It was first found in 2009 in a patient's ear in Japan and has spread to hospitals around the world. Many strains resist common antifungal drugs, and it clings to surfaces for weeks.

name: Bdelloid Rotifer
entry: Bdelloid rotifers have had no males for tens of millions of years. They borrow genes from bacteria and fungi to stay healthy. In 2021, a bdelloid was revived after 24,000 years in Siberian permafrost.

name: Loriciferan
range: Oxygen-free brine at the bottom of the Mediterranean
entry: It was found in a deep, salty basin with no oxygen at all. It may be the first animal known to live its whole life without oxygen, though scientists still debate the finding.

name: C. elegans
entry: Every adult hermaphrodite has exactly 959 cells, and scientists have mapped every one of its 302 neurons. Worms carried on space shuttle Columbia survived its breakup in 2003.

name: Permafrost Nematode
entry: In 2018, scientists revived worms that had been frozen in Siberian permafrost for about 46,000 years, since the time of the Neanderthals. They started moving and reproducing again.

name: Vinegar Eel
entry: This tiny worm lives in raw, unfiltered vinegar and feeds on the bacteria that make it. Thousands wriggle together in a jar, and swarms of them can even move in sync. Aquarium keepers use them as live fish food.

name: House Dust Mite
entry: It lives in beds, pillows and carpets, eating the flakes of skin people shed. It does not bite. Its droppings are a common cause of allergies and asthma.

name: Face Mite
entry: Most adults have these tiny mites living head-down in the hair follicles of their faces. They eat skin oil and come out at night to crawl across the skin and mate.

name: Water Flea
entry: Its body is see-through, so you can watch its heart beat. When it smells chemicals from predators, it grows protective spines and a helmet. Females can make clones without males.

name: Salmon Parasite
entry: This tiny relative of jellyfish lives in salmon muscles. In 2020, scientists discovered it has no mitochondrial genome, making it the first animal known that does not use oxygen to make energy.

name: Trichoplax
entry: It is one of the simplest animals, a flat blob only a few cells thick with no organs, nerves or muscles. It glides over algae, digesting food by settling on top of it.

name: Fairyfly
entry: The males of this wasp are the smallest known insects, smaller than some single-celled organisms. They are blind and wingless and never leave the beetle egg where they hatched.

name: Sea-Monkey
entry: This brine shrimp lays eggs that can dry out and survive for years. Add salt water and they hatch, which is why they were sold as instant pets called Sea-Monkeys.

name: Speed Mite
entry: For its size, it is the fastest land animal known. It runs up to 322 body lengths per second on hot concrete. A human running that fast would be moving over 1,300 miles per hour.

name: Whirling Disease Parasite
entry: This tiny relative of jellyfish infects young trout, damaging their spines and nerves. Infected fish swim in endless circles, chasing their own tails.

name: Gastrotrich
entry: This tiny animal glides on a carpet of beating hairs on its belly. Its back is covered in spines and scales. It lives only a few days to a few weeks.

name: Bacteriophage T4
entry: It looks like a tiny lunar lander. It lands on a bacterium with its spider-like legs and injects its DNA like a syringe. Within half an hour, the bacterium bursts, releasing over 100 new viruses.

name: Tobacco Mosaic Virus
entry: It was the first virus ever discovered, in the 1890s, when scientists found that something smaller than bacteria was spotting tobacco leaves. It is a stiff rod and can stay infectious for decades.

name: Mimivirus
entry: It is so large that it was first mistaken for a bacterium, which is why its name means mimicking microbe. It is bigger than some bacteria and has more genes than some living cells.

name: Pithovirus
entry: This giant, jar-shaped virus was found frozen in 30,000-year-old Siberian soil. In 2014, scientists thawed it and it infected amoebae again. It only infects amoebae, not people.

name: Tulip Breaking Virus
entry: It streaks tulip petals with feathery flames of color. In the 1630s, these striped tulips were so prized in the Netherlands that single bulbs sold for more than a house, an event called tulip mania.

name: Sputnik Virophage
entry: It is a virus that infects other viruses. It can only multiply inside an amoeba that is already infected with a giant virus, and it hijacks the giant virus's machinery, weakening it.

name: Syncytin Retrovirus
range: Inside the DNA of every human
entry: Millions of years ago, a virus inserted its genes into the DNA of our ancestors. One of those viral genes now makes syncytin, a protein that helps build the placenta. Without it, mammals as we know them might not exist.

name: Pandoravirus
range: Water & mud; first found off the coast of Chile
entry: This giant virus is about a micrometer long, bigger than many bacteria. It has around 2,500 genes, and most of them look like nothing else known in nature, which is why it was named after Pandora's box.

name: Chlorovirus ATCV-1
entry: This virus normally infects green algae in lakes. In 2014, scientists were surprised to find it in the throats of some healthy people, and one study linked it to slightly slower thinking on some tests.

name: Myxoma Virus
range: Rabbits in South America, Australia & Europe
entry: It causes a mild disease in South American rabbits but is deadly to European rabbits. Australia released it in 1950 to control invasive rabbits. Over time, the virus became milder and the rabbits more resistant.
